Rear window,
Rear sash found raised nine and one-quarter inches and jammed there on a frayed cord. Paint scuffed along the inside edge of the sill and a thread of dark wool caught on the catch.
No damage to the frame and no tool marks: the sash was not forced any further than it stood. Whoever came through it came through it as it was.
Corridor door,
Door frame split along the jamb at fifty-eight inches from the floor on the strike side. The split is fresh and runs outward, consistent with a shoulder driven against the frame from the corridor.
No tool marks. The lock held; the wood did not. It takes weight to do this to oak.
Preliminary findings,
Arterial spatter on the north wall arcs from a point of origin no lower than seventy-four inches from the floor. The deceased stood five foot four in stockings.
The assailant faced her and stood over her, and the blow was delivered downward from well above her head.
Trace examination, item 1
Not the deceased's: hers is dyed auburn and shows it at the roots. This one has never seen a bottle. Caught in the setting when the ring hand was raised.
Lifted from the inside of the collar, which means a head was close over hers. The deceased's hair is dark; nobody on the hotel staff is fair.
One red hair on the pillow, and nobody else in the building with a head like that. Copper, unmistakable, and not out of a bottle.
Trace examination, items 1–7
Pulled out in the struggle, by the roots. The deceased was twenty-six and had not a grey hair on her. These came off the other head in the room.
A single blow to the right temple. The track runs downward and toward the left side of the skull, entering at some thirty degrees from the front.
Bruising on her left forearm where she raised it. The assailant stood square in front of her when the blow was struck.
Trace examination, item 3
Powder residue on the outer index finger and the web of the thumb, consistent with a small-calibre discharge. The interior is worn through at the fingertips: an old glove, and the working one.
Trace examination, item 5
She marked whoever she fought. Among the fresh tissue under her nails is a fleck of old scar: fibrous, pale, years healed. She scratched somebody who had already been cut once.
Statement of the night lift attendant
"The hand came down on her shoulder and the cuff rode up. There was ink on the wrist. Blue. A picture, not letters — something with a curl to it."
"I did not see a face. I see hands all night; I could not tell you a face if you paid me."
Plate 4: tumbler, sideboard
Print lifted from the dust on the sideboard where the tumbler was set down. Palm and four fingers, clear. Not a partial: the surface is clean where a fifth finger should have rested.
Statement of the night clerk
"Ordinary. That is what I keep telling you. Nothing on the face, nothing on the hands, no mark I could point to. You could not pick them out of a line of ten."
"I would know them again. I could not tell you why."
Pencilled chit
"I.O.U. $40 — Wed. — Rosie's." Creased in half, stepped on, and dropped in the struggle. Nobody who does not play carries a marker from Rosie's.
Plate 2: two glasses, the table
Two glasses. Hers has the lipstick. The other has a ring of rye still in it and a thumbprint we cannot match. The deceased kept no rye in the suite; somebody brought their own.
Trace examination, item 8
Somebody in that room smoked a pipe that was not tobacco, and recently. The soot at the sill is from a small lamp. The deceased did not use; her doctor is emphatic.
Inventory,
Whoever spent the evening here left nothing of a habit behind, because they have none. In this city that is rarer than a fingerprint.
Trace examination, item 6
The curtains and her lapel are saturated with it. The deceased did not smoke, and the hotel sells Turkish. Somebody stood close to her for a long time with the cheap stuff on their coat.
Orchid, laid on thick and transferred by contact. Not hers: she wore jasmine and nothing else. Somebody stood very close.
Plate 6: brass push-plate, corridor door
A thumbprint in machine oil on the brass. Somebody who works with machines and never quite gets it off, whatever they scrub with.
Trace examination, item 7
Faint, sickly, hanging over the pillow. Hospital ether, which nobody buys in a shop.
Cast no. 1, flowerbed below the window
A neat impression pressed into the flowerbed, the heel narrow. Shallow, too: not a heavy tread.
Cast no. 1, the yard
A plain sole, worn down hard on the outer heel: somebody who walks a great deal and walks badly.
Cast no. 1, wet ash by the back stair
Pressed deep into the wet ash by the back stair. Twelve inches even, and a heel like a brick.
In a dead man's handwriting
Folded four times and soft at the creases. "If anything happens to me —
The rest is water.

The second cup was still warm when the chair emptied.

11:50 PM — R. VOSS — box 114 — signed out 11:58. The signature is hurried and the pen dug through the page.
Miss Vine remembers the hand that signed, and what it looked like doing it.
Fare chit no. 88
The driver is still on the rank outside, and he knows a way up the Bluff that is not on any map.
Calls placed from the Gilded, suite 1100
12:52 AM — outgoing — LANTERN 4-4 — duration one minute ten. The last call the suite ever made.
Quill wrote the number down when she should not have.
Effects of the deceased, Voss, L.
A brass key stamped one-fourteen in the pocket of a woman with no purse to spend. The morgue does not guess what it opens. You are allowed to.
The eleven o'clock spot, Nov. 3
Vera Lang on the little stage at eleven, in the flash. The house photographer sells these at the door for a dollar. This one was not bought; it was taken.
You can see a great deal of a person in a flash photograph.
Consignment, SS Marseillaise
Forty crates, orchids, Marseille to Ashgrave. Twenty-eight initialled at the dock by the bond clerk. Twelve initialled by somebody else, in the importer's own hand, at the warehouse, at night.
She signed for them herself. The clerk remembers the hand.
Entries, Nov. 3
10:05 PM — ether, four oz. — signed A. PIKE — purpose: "surgical". The signature is his, the chemist says, and the hand that made it he has watched a thousand times.
Tag no. 9
A coat, wet through, hung in locker nine at half past two and never claimed. In the pocket, a second locker tag from somewhere else in the city.
Collections, week of Nov. 3
Every entry in Brandt's hand, and every hand that paid him remembered by the man who keeps the book. He knows more about the collector than the collector knows about himself.
Seal broken, bay 4
A crate went out without paper, and the cart tracks in the wet lead out of the yard and up the road.
To Roland, unfinished
"Rollo — I have changed the will and I have told Father's lawyer why. When you read this you will already know. I am sorry it had to be me who—"
The pen stops. The rest of the page is clean.
Lights on the Bluff, night of Nov. 3

2:30 — lantern on the cliff path, stops at the old stair, returns. 2:55 — lantern again, further out. 3:10 — nothing. The keeper thinks it was the fishermen. You will have to go and look to be sure it was not, and it costs you an hour to find out it was.
Certificate of death, Bask, A.
Signed twice by the same hand forty minutes apart. The first entry is written in a hurry and struck through with one line. The second is written slowly.
Kite, the attendant, notes in the margin that the doctor stood with the body for the whole forty minutes in between and did not speak.
Manifest, SS Corvina

Six weeks of crates, every page initialled by the inspector and not one crate opened. A second set of initials has been added over hers tonight, in a different pen, by somebody who knew her initials but not her hand.
Traffic, night of the 11th
Three messages, logged in the operator's hand, the last one underlined twice.
Ticket no. 3391
Okafor's knife, pledged in March so he could eat, and bought back the night before the murder by a stranger with Okafor's ticket in his hand.
To Tilda, 1941, never sent
"If I end up in the water it was not the water. Ask Bask. He knows who on this boat wants me gone, and he will be at the wheel. — A."
Kept seven years in a drawer, read so often the folds have gone soft.
The 11th, evening
The last sale of the day, at closing. The chandler signed for it himself, which he never does, and the apprentice watched a stranger's hand rest on top of his while he did it.
Longshoremen's Local, account 40
One withdrawal in a year of deposits, two days before the vote, with the purpose line empty.
Plate 2: right side, the deceased
The blade entered under the right ribs and travelled upward toward the heart. Whoever held it was below him, on the ladder or in a boat, looking up.
Tag no. 17
The coat was never collected. The man who left it ran when the attendant found the key.
Tag, net 6, MARIE-LOUISE
A brass net tag, stamped for the Marie-Louise, fished out of the water under Pier Nine at low tide by the man who found the body. The Marie-Louise carries no nets.
Fixes, 11:15 PM and 11:50 PM
Bearings taken from the tower and plotted. The rowing boat went under the pier and came out again thirty-five minutes later.
February, spring tides
A pencil mark against low water on the 12th. That is when the pier gave him up. Nothing else on the page.
Six weeks of landings
A tally kept by the man who carried the crates, in a hand that learned to write in Rotterdam. Every landing at the ice house steps, and one line for the 11th that is not about crates.
A. Bask — twenty years

Tea every morning for twenty years at a penny a day, paid every Friday. The last line, in Nell Mott's hand: "10th — sat with D.H. an hour, argued about a name. Wrote a note on my paper and took it with him."
Account, the Rectory, April
Twelve of sherry, six of port, and a note from the merchant: "Canon — the crypt fund cheque was returned again. We must ask." Mrs. Tull has watched him drink the twelve.
Interments, 1939

Plot forty-four: a name, a date, a fee of forty pounds, and the page it was on razored out tonight. The stub is still in the binding, and Miss Pym knows which page it was because she gave it to Constance last week.
Whoever cut it left a fingerprint in the glue.
Plate 3: the verger's key board

Forty hooks, thirty-nine keys, and the empty hook labelled TOWER in the verger's hand. In the flash, the verger himself, caught in the doorway, and something about him the constable did not notice at the time.
To the Dean, unposted

"...I must therefore report that Mr. Blake has been seen with the boys of the third form at the Observatory after lights out on three occasions, and that Dr. Quint has declined to say what they were shown. — C. Ayre." Sealed, stamped, never posted, and found in the desk of the man it names.
Entries, April
Chloral hydrate, two drachms, signed S. CRAKE, for Marrow House, the 8th. Miss Lamb watched her sign, as she has watched her sign every month for eleven years.
Sign-out, night of the 9th
Car 7 — out 00:02 — R. FAY — back 00:51 — "wet". The dispatcher did not sign it and does not know how she got the key. He watched her bring it back, and what she did with her hands while he asked.
Valve keys, the 9th

Key 3 out at 23:50 against the Canon's standing order, returned 03:00 with initials that are not his. The walkway it opens runs along the top of the reservoir wall, and the wet prints on it run one way.
Crypt restoration fund
Four hundred pounds gone from a box with one signature on every slip. Constance had asked to see the box on Thursday. On Friday she was dead.
Plate 9: the bell tower, from the water tower

Taken at dawn with a long lens: the tower, the stair window, and on the outside of the tower a line of iron rungs the diocese had forgotten about, running from the ringing floor to the ground. The bottom rung is bright where the rust has been worn off tonight.
One glove, left hand
A woman's glove, left hand, grey kid, left on a chair after words at four in the morning. Mrs. Petty saw the hand that took it off. She also saw the hand it belonged to, and the difference.

A single wound under the right ribs. The track runs upward and across to the deceased's left, toward the heart. The assailant was below him, facing him, on the ladder or in a boat.

Both pockets sewn shut with the same over-and-over stitch, worked from right to left with the knot finished on the right. That is how a right-handed man sews sailcloth: needle in the right hand, cloth held in the left, the work moving toward the left.
A left-handed man sews the other way, and finishes on the other side.

The deceased got a hand on whoever was below him. Under the nails of the right hand: skin, blood, and a hard white fleck that is old scar tissue, the kind that comes away from a badly healed wound when it is clawed.

"There was a boat under Pier Nine with no light. A hand came up and took hold of the ladder rail, and the sleeve went back, and there was blue on the wrist. Ink. Like the navy men have. I didn't see a face. I saw the wrist."

Wedged under the thwart of the boat found drifting under the pier. A marker from Teague's Thursday game, damp and creased from a pocket. The deceased did not play; he said so loudly and often.

, the ladder head

A half bottle of dark rum pushed down between the boards at the ladder head, cork out, a third gone. It was not there at the evening tide; the pier man swears to it. The deceased drank stout at the Brine every night of his life and nothing else.

The canvas cover from the boat reeks of sweet smoke, and a warm knife against it brings the smell up strong. Somebody sat under that canvas and smoked a pipe before they rowed. The harbour has two places that sell it and both are shut by ten.
Contents of the boat found under

Turned out to the boards. A sailmaker's needle, an empty spool of waxed thread, a spilled pound of rock salt and the blood. Not a bottle, not a butt, not a card. Two hours in a boat on a February night and nothing to warm the hands.

Even after the harbour, the collar and left shoulder of his oilskin smell of orchid perfume. It is laid on thick and it was laid on close: somebody with that scent on them held him by the collar and shoulder, or was held.

, ladder rail, developed

The waxed thread from the pockets smells of ether, and wax holds a smell. It came from the hands: whoever pulled those stitches tight had ether on their fingers, the sweet sharp smell of a hospital corridor or a dispensary shelf.

A drawn cut lays the fibres over in the direction the blade travelled. These are laid from right to left as you face the rope from the stairs, with the last strands torn on the left.

The cord is tied with the hitch the Company teaches its lamplighters for the ladder, but mirrored: the working end crosses left over the standing part. A right-handed man ties it the other way without thinking, as the Company manual shows.

"He held the sixpence out and his sleeve went up and there was blue on his wrist. Ink. Like the sailors at the canal have. I looked at it instead of his face because it was the only thing in the light. Then he said run, so I ran."

The lighthouse keeper watches us land. He waves. Then he goes inside and writes.
What did you see from the deck?

We anchored in the Narrows at ten past eleven with the lights off. The skipper took the dinghy to Pier Nine at a quarter past to fetch a passenger for Salvi. He came back at ten to twelve alone, wet to the waist, and said the passenger hadn't shown. Then we went out to the Corvina.
Wet to the waist.
He said he'd slipped off the ladder. He sat in the bow all the way out and didn't say another word. And something went over the side off the pier before he rowed back. A sack. It floated.
Where did the sack go?
With the tide, toward the salt works. It washed up on the outfall pipe. It had the works' stencil on it, and it was empty.
What's in the hold?
Nobody has ever told me. I've smelled it. It isn't fish. It's whatever the cannery cans when there aren't any fish.
Who else was aboard that night?

The Corvina's mate. Dutch, we call him. He came ashore six weeks ago and never went back. He sleeps in the old salt stairs under the lighthouse, where the boats land without lights. Nobody at your station knows he exists. He was on deck with me when the skipper rowed off.
Nell Harrow. I hand out the towels and take the tickets. Nobody has pockets in here. That's why they talk.
They bathe here. You can't hide much in a towel.
A coat was left in locker seventeen with something heavy sewn into the lining. Its owner ran off toward
We close at two. That's all I have.
Miss Wren bathes on Tuesdays and cries in the steam room where she thinks nobody can hear.
Mrs. Rask hasn't been in since 1941. Her husband bathed here every Friday.
Garrow comes down from the lighthouse once a month and sits in the hot room like a man trying to boil something off himself.
Who came through the baths?

A man in an oilskin at half past four in the morning, wet to the waist, with his hands wrapped in a rag. He wanted the hot room and wouldn't take a towel. He left his coat in locker seventeen with something sewn into the lining.
What was sewn in the lining?
A key, stamped 'Bond Store 12'. He ran when he saw I'd found it. He ran toward the Narrows, where the trawlers tie up.
Did Bask bathe here?
Every Friday for twenty years. On the 10th he sat in the hot room and told me the union was about to find out what it had been carrying. I thought he meant the dues.
Ruth Gault. I log the boats. In, out, weight, captain. When the log and the water disagree, I write down what the water says.
They come to my counter. You learn a person by how they lie about the weight of their cargo.
A boat went out at eleven with no cargo declared and came back at three sitting low in the water. Ask what came off her at
The office is closed. The log is locked.
Miss Wren's stamps and my log should agree. Since the Corvina came in, they haven't once.
Salvi declares his cargo weights the way some men declare their age.
Garrow and I keep the same log from opposite ends of the harbour. Mine is honest. His is crossed out.
What moved on the 11th?

The Marie-Louise out at eleven with no cargo declared. Back at five past three, sitting low in the water, at the ice house steps and not her berth. High tide at 1:40. I wrote 'low?' with a question mark. The question mark is mine.
Sitting low with what?
Corvina cargo, for the ice house. Ask the ice man what came off her. Ask the lighthouse keeper what he crossed out.
Bask came to this office.
On the 9th. He read six weeks of boat movements and copied every Marie-Louise entry into a notebook. He said: Ruth, you've been writing it all down. I said somebody had to.
They call me Sparks. Real name's Tomasz. Every wireless message on the water comes through these headphones. Most of them are about fish. Most.
They send messages through me. You can tell a person by the way they tap a key.
A message went out to a boat at one in the morning: 'STOP AT THE USUAL PLACE.' I don't know where that is. I know the man who sent it was seen at
I have a ship calling. It isn't you.
Garrow has no wireless. He doesn't need one. He has a lamp and a grudge.
Salvi's messages are all about fish, and not one of them ever names a fish.
Ledoux taps a key slowly and heavily, like a man who doesn't want to be understood.
What went over the wireless?

At 1:04, from the shipping office to the Marie-Louise: STOP AT THE USUAL PLACE. At 1:06 the reply: UNDERSTOOD. At 3:12, from the Marie-Louise: ALL DONE. I underlined that last one twice, because I know what it usually means, and tonight I'm not sure I do.
Where is the usual place?
The ice house steps. Every boat that lands without Customs lands there. Ask the ice man what came off her tonight, and who.
Did Bask send anything?
On the 10th, to the union's city office: ONE MORE THING TO CHECK, THEN I NAME THEM. I sent it. I haven't slept since.
Mabel Brack. I clean the hall after the meetings. I've cleaned up after every man who ever wanted to run this union.
They sit in that hall every Thursday. I've swept around their feet for years.
The back office was opened at one with a key that wasn't the vice-chairman's. The heel prints went out toward
The hall is locked. I'm going home.
Dov left at midnight with the committee. He was the last to sign the minutes and his hand was shaking.
Mrs. Rask has had a key to this hall since 1941. Nobody ever took it back. She has never used it.
Bernard came to the hall on the 10th to beg Bask for more time. Bask gave him a week. He didn't need a week.
What happened at the hall?

The election committee until midnight. Then quiet. Then at one o'clock somebody opened the back office with a key that wasn't the vice-chairman's, and left with Bask's little notebook. There was mud on the floor from a woman's heel. Small. Neat.
What notebook?
The one he wrote the boats down in. He kept it in the back office behind a new padlock. Whoever has it has the whole harbour in their pocket. The heel prints went out toward Customs Row.
Twenty years. What was he like?
He never once sat down in this hall. He stood at the back like a man who didn't expect to be allowed to stay.
Émile Delacroix. I set the type for the union newspaper. I know every word before the union does, and I know who wanted which words changed.
They bring me their articles. You learn a person by what they cross out.
Somebody pulled a notice from tomorrow's paper at five past midnight and walked out with his hands shaking, toward
The press is running. Mind your fingers on the way out.
Hollis came in at five past midnight and pulled the chairman's notice with his own key. He said the chairman had changed his mind. His hands were shaking.
Mrs. Rask places a notice every year on the anniversary of her husband's death. This year she placed it early.
What was pulled from the newspaper?

Bask's notice: 'The Chairman will address the membership on the matter of the Corvina and the trawler berths.' Set in type, proofed, and pulled at five past midnight by Dov Hollis with his own key. He said the chairman had changed his mind.
Had he?
Bask never changed his mind about anything in twenty years. I set the notice again at six in the morning. Then Kite telephoned and I took it down for good.
Did Bask write for the paper?
Every week for twenty years. Plain words, short lines. The last thing he wrote was: 'If I am not at the vote, ask why.'
Femi Oyelaran. I've guarded these crates for six weeks. In six weeks nobody came for them. Until tonight.
They come to look at the seals. You learn a person by how they look at a seal they aren't allowed to break.
One crate was opened at nine and closed again, badly. Whatever came out of it went along the quay to
I have crates to watch. I'm watching them.
Miss Wren signs at the door and never comes inside. I've offered her a lamp. She's never taken it.
Salvi's name is on the manifest, on the seals, and on the envelope he leaves for me. I haven't opened it.
Ledoux breaks a customs seal the way other men open a bottle of beer.
Which crate was opened?
Bay four, seal number 2216. One twist. Ledoux did it at nine in the evening, on Salvi's orders, before he sailed. He took out a small case and carried it to the shipping office.
What was in the case?
I don't open crates. I know what a crate of morphine ampoules sounds like when it's set down, and that one sounded like it. It went to Salvi. Whatever else happened tonight, that happened first.
Bask came to the bond store.
On the 9th. He asked me what was in the crates. I said I was only a watchman. He said: then watch. I've been watching ever since.
Nan Mott. Tea is a penny. For another penny I'll tell you who drank it. Bask drank his tea here every morning for twenty years.
They take tea here. I've set a cup in front of them a thousand times.
Bask wrote a note on my paper on the 10th and carried it off. It named a place, and a time. Before he went there, he stopped at
The kettle's off. So am I.
Dov sat with Bask for an hour on the 10th and left angry. Bask stayed and didn't touch his tea.
Bernard was here until ten on the 11th with a cup he didn't drink and a face like a debt.
The doctor takes tea here at six, after a night shift. On the 12th she didn't come.
Okafor until ten. Then nobody. It was the quietest night in a year. I remember thinking the whole harbour was holding its breath.
Bask left the Brine with a note on your café paper.

He wrote it here on the 10th, at that table, and folded it in four. I read it upside down; I read everything upside down. It said: Pier Nine, half past eleven, Thursday's proof. He'll show me the hold. That was all.
Twenty years of tea.
A penny a day. He never once asked for credit. On the 10th he sat with Hollis and they argued about a name. Not Hollis's name. Somebody Bask was going to name out loud on Thursday.
Aldo Penrose. I polish the brass plaque and read out the names of the drowned. There's a new name on it this week, in chalk. I didn't write it.
They come to the plaque. You learn a person by which name they touch.
Somebody knelt here at half past one and left a key in the charity box. She came in from the direction of
The chapel is open to everyone. Everyone except you, tonight.
Mrs. Rask comes every anniversary and touches one name on the plaque. This year she came at half past four in the morning and wrote a second one.
Garrow hasn't set foot inside the chapel since 1941. He stands in the doorway.
Who wrote the chalk name?
The widow, at half past four in the morning. Sand on her boots from the point. Somebody had told her, and she came to write it before it was even true.
Something was left in the charity box.

A padlock key, a big new one. A woman came in at half past one, knelt for a long time without praying, and left it. Whoever broke into that union office put the key where a priest would find it. Guilt, I think. Not a joke.
Tell me about Ambrose Rask.
First name on the plaque under 1941. Bask paid for the plaque. He came every year and stood in front of it. He never prayed. He wasn't a praying man. He was a remembering one.
Jean Sable, Coastguard. I log every boat that crosses the Narrows after dark. I also know which ones aren't in the log.
They pass under my telescope. You learn a person by how they stand at a wheel.
A rowing boat with no lights went under Pier Nine at a quarter past eleven and came out at ten to twelve. The trawler it came from tied up later at
The watch changes at six. Ask somebody else.
Garrow and I watch the same water. He writes down what he's paid to. I write down what I see. We've never compared notes.
Ledoux stands at his wheel like a man who's been told where to go and would rather not.
What crossed the Narrows?

The Marie-Louise in at ten past eleven with no lights, anchored off Pier Nine. A rowing boat from her to the pier at a quarter past, one man in it. The rowing boat back at ten to twelve, one man in it. Then she went out at midnight and came back at three to the ice house steps.
Tell me about the one man.
An oilskin, hood up, rowing well. He went under the pier and I lost him in the dark. When he came back he sat in the bow of the trawler and didn't move. Garrow saw the same. Garrow crossed it out.
Did Bask ever come to the tower?
On the 9th. He asked to see six weeks of crossings. I gave them to him. He said: so it's all written down. I said: it always was. Nobody ever asked.
Nurse Ives. I run Dr. Fenn's wards. I run them better than she runs her paperwork.
They've been through my ward. You don't forget a patient. Or a visitor.
A man came to the door on the 12th with his fingers cut to ribbons and said it was rope. He went back toward
I'm doing my rounds. If you're not bleeding, out.
Dr. Fenn went out at half past five, when the morgue telephoned, and came back at half past six with her hands washed and her face like a wall.
Mr. Hollis has a weak heart. He came in on the 10th with palpitations and wouldn't say what had caused them.
Bernard Okafor came in on the 12th with cuts across his fingers. He said it was rope. Rope doesn't cut like that. Canvas does.
What came into the Infirmary on the 11th?
Nothing. That's what I remember. The quietest night of the winter. Then at half past five the telephone, and the doctor went white and took her bag.
Tell me about Okafor's hands.

Cut across the pads of the fingers, both hands, the way sailmakers cut themselves when they sew without a leather palm. He said rope. The doctor let him say it. She stitched three fingers and didn't ask.
Bask was here on the 11th.
At ten, for half an hour, with the doctor, and not as a patient. When he left she sat in the dispensary and didn't move for a long time. She told me afterwards he had a boat to meet.
Bram Cully. I cut the ice and stack it. A trawler unloaded at my steps at three this morning, and afterwards a man sat in my cold room with his hands in the ice.
They buy ice from me. You learn a person by what they need to keep cold.
A man sat in my cold room at four with his hands in the ice. When he left he went toward
Ice doesn't wait. Neither do I.
Ledoux unloads into my ice house at three in the morning. I don't cut the blocks he uses.
Salvi buys ice for a shipping office. Shipping offices don't need ice. Unless they do.
What came through the ice house?

Corvina cargo off the Marie-Louise from a quarter past three until four. Two blocks of ice for Salvi's back room. And a man who sat in the cold room afterwards for a quarter of an hour with his coat off and his hands in the ice.
Why the ice?

His hands were cut. Both of them, across the fingers, like a man who's been sewing canvas without a palm. The crew keep their hoods up in here and I don't look at faces. He went out toward the point, toward the Rask house.
On the 9th. He walked through the cold room, counted the crates, and wrote in a notebook. He said: Bram, this isn't fish. I said: no, it isn't.
Ma Lundy. Everything in this harbour ends up in my shop window sooner or later. On the 10th something went out of it that I wish I had kept.
They pawn things with me. I look at their hands.
A pawn ticket was paid off on the 10th, in cash, by somebody who wasn't the person who pawned the item. They went toward
The shop is shut. I've said more than I should.
Bernard pawned his knife in March so he could eat. He couldn't have bought it back. He sold the ticket instead, and I know it, because a stranger brought it in.
Mrs. Rask pawned her wedding ring in 1942, bought it back in 1943, and hasn't been in since.
Ledoux pawns nothing. A man who never needs money is a man who's paid in cash.
Who bought back the knife?

A man in an oilskin, on the evening of the 10th, the night before, with Okafor's ticket and cash. Hood up. He paid with a banknote that smelled of fish. He didn't say a word, and I look at hands, not faces: big hands, no rings, salt in the knuckles.
Where did he go?
Down the row toward the trawler berths, with the knife inside his coat and his hand on it.
Did Bask ever pawn anything?
Never. He came in on the 10th and bought something: a sailmaker's needle from the tray. He said it was for mending a coat. I thought nothing of it. Now I think of nothing else.
Tamsin Rook. I'm the conductor on the last tram along the quay at midnight. I punch the tickets, and I remember the people who'd rather I didn't.
They ride my tram. You learn a person by where they refuse to sit.
Somebody rode to the end of the line at half past nine and didn't ride back. Later I saw the same coat going toward
The tram's in the shed. So am I.
Mr. Hollis rode to the union hall at eight on the 11th and didn't ride back. He walked. Slowly.
The doctor never takes the tram. She walks to the Infirmary at six every evening with her bag. On the 11th she was on time.
Miss Wren rides home at eleven every night. She sits at the front and doesn't look at anyone.
Who rode the tram on the 11th?
At half past nine a man in an oilskin rode to the end of the line, the salt works, and wasn't on the car back. Miss Wren at eleven, at the front, looking at nobody. Nobody after that.
Tell me about the one who didn't ride back.

Hood up. Paid with coins that were wet. He got off at the works and walked toward the kilns. Later, coming back down the lane at ten, I saw a man with a sack on his shoulder go toward the quay. Same coat. I can't swear it was the same man.
Did Bask ride the tram?
Every night for twenty years, standing at the back. On the 11th he didn't. I noticed. I didn't say anything. Who would I have said it to?
Jack Orme. I bag salt. A hundredweight a bag, six hundred bags a night. Tonight I'm one bag short.
They come here for salt. You learn a person by how much they can carry.
The missing bag went out on somebody's shoulder at ten. That somebody walked down the lane toward
The kilns need feeding. You don't.
Okafor buys salt for his shop by the bag. He hasn't bought a bag since March.
Ledoux buys salt by the ton, for fish he doesn't catch.
You're one bag short.
Carried out on a man's shoulder at ten o'clock, off the stack by the kiln door. No cart. A man in an oilskin. He walked down the lane toward the quay as if it weighed nothing.
Where does the lane go?
Through the gate and down to Pier Nine, if you keep walking. He kept walking. The sack came back to me on the outfall pipe the next morning, empty.
Did Bask ever come to the salt works?
On the 9th. He stood by the kilns and asked me who buys rock salt by the hundredweight. I said: fishermen. He said: name one.
Sam Cotter. I found him. I was under the pier at low water for the crab pots and there he was, face down, heavy as a church.
I see them on the water. You learn a man by how he handles a boat.
The tide took something off him before it gave him up. It fetched up along the shore near
I've said it three times now. I need to sit down.
Ledoux anchors off this pier some nights with his lights out. I've seen his dinghy go under the boards. I thought it was women.
Garrow's lamp went round all night the same as always. Whatever he saw, he saw it.
Okafor sold me every pot I own on credit. He's a good man with no luck.
What did you find?
Him. Ten to five, low water, under the ladder. Pockets sewn up and heavy with salt. And a brass net tag in the mud beside him, stamped for the Marie-Louise. I gave the tag to the berth master.
Tell me about the ladder.

The storm boards are up for the winter; you go through the gap. Somebody had been down that ladder in the night. There was salt spilled on the boards at the top and a smear of blood on the lamp bracket. I didn't touch either. I know better.
Did you know Bask?
He got me my pension when the union didn't want to. I pulled him out of the water like a sack of salt and I'm not ashamed I cried.
Brother Fry. Forty beds and a stove. I count the men in at ten and count them again in the morning. The numbers don't always match.
They sleep here sometimes. You learn a person by what they say in their sleep.
Garrow came down from his tower at five in the morning and said he had crossed something out. What he crossed out was near
The men are sleeping. Keep your voice down and go.
Mrs. Rask sends blankets every winter with her husband's name sewn into them. I unpick the name. She knows I do.
Garrow sleeps here when the lighthouse gets too much for him. He talks in his sleep about a boat.
Dov Hollis paid for the mission's coal last winter out of his own pocket and told nobody. I tell people.
Who came to the mission on the 11th?
Nobody new. Twelve regulars. Garrow came down from the lighthouse at five in the morning, which he never does on a working night, and sat by the stove with his boots on.
What did Garrow say?
He said: Nora, I crossed something out and I shouldn't have. Then he said nothing for an hour and went back up. If you want what he crossed out, it's in his tower, under the boards.
Did Bask come to the mission?
He paid for the stove every winter. He never came inside. He stood at the door, counted the beds through the window, and left.
The skipper pays me. That is all I know about him and all I want to know.
Salvi signs my money. He has never once looked at my face.
Okafor sold me rope once and asked me where I slept. Nobody else ever has.
The lighthouse man sees me land every time. He has never come down the stairs.
The union man? Never met him. The union does not come down here.
The customs woman signs the papers for the crates I carry. She has never seen me either.
The old woman on the point leaves bread on her wall for me. She thinks I do not know it is her.
The doctor stitched my hand in December and did not charge me. I have not forgotten.
Where were you on the 11th?
On the Marie-Louise. We anchored off the pier with the lights off. The skipper took the boat in. We waited. Then we went out to the Corvina and came back full. That is every night, more or less.
A man in an oilskin redeemed Okafor's knife at Lundy's on the 10th.
He is quiet for a long time. Me. The skipper gave me the ticket and two dollars and said to fetch it. I fetched it and gave it to him on the quay. I thought it was a knife. It was a knife.
Somebody paid you to forget that night.

Fifty dollars. From the skipper, at the ice house steps, at four in the morning, with his hands wrapped in a rag. He said: you saw nothing. I said: I saw nothing. I am saying it now because you have found me, and because Bask wrote my name down in his book and I would like somebody to cross it out.
What is in the crates?
Morphine. Swiss watches. Whatever Salvi is paid to move. I carry it. I do not open it. That is the whole of my job and the whole of my crime.
Etta Wren signs whatever she's told to sign. She has a neat hand for it.
Bernard owes money to everyone and pays nobody. Bask called in his debt on the 9th. That was cruel.
Salvi buys people. He bought half the union hall. He never tried to buy me. He never even offered.
Tilda Rask has hated Bask for seven years and me for eleven. She's fair about it.
Garrow sees everything from the lighthouse. He has never given evidence about any of it.
The doctor and Bask were closer than the harbour knows. I knew.
Ledoux goes out empty and comes back full. Bask was writing it all down. I told him not to.
Where were you on the night of the 11th?
At the union hall with the election committee until midnight. Then I walked to the printers, then the Brine until one, then home. My wife will confirm the last part. Mags Teague the middle.
You were second in command for eleven years. On Thursday you become the boss.
Only because he's dead. I didn't want it this way. I wanted him to step down and shake my hand.
Four hundred dollars came out of the union account on the 10th, with your signature.
He rubs his face. I paid a man to stand down from the election. He took the money and ran against me anyway. I stole from the union and I still lost. Print that.
You pulled Bask's notice from the paper at five past midnight.

I did. He was going to name Ledoux, Salvi and the Corvina in print, in front of three thousand men, two days before a vote. I thought it would start a war on the quay. I told the printer the chairman had changed his mind. He hadn't. He was already in the water, and I didn't know it.
What was Bask like?
Hard. Fair. He never forgave anything. He knew who put Ambrose Rask in the bay, and he kept it to himself for seven years like a coin in his pocket.
Hollis is an honest man in a job with no room for one.
Okafor sells rope to the Corvina's crews and pretends not to know what they tie up with it.
Salvi is polite. Salvi pays on time. Salvi is the worst thing in this harbour.
The widow came to the Customs House in 1941 with a question about a boat. Nobody answered her. I was a clerk then. I didn't answer either.
Garrow writes down what he's paid to and crosses out the rest. He and I are the same, and I hate him for it.
Dr. Fenn signed my father's death certificate. Quickly, and correctly. I owe her for that.
Ledoux's boat is listed on my manifests as a fishing vessel. I have never seen a fish on it.
At the Customs House until eleven. Aldous, the clerk, saw me leave. I took the tram home. I live alone.
Six weeks of crates. Every page signed by you. Not one crate opened.
That's right. I sign. I don't open. Ask me why and I'll tell you, and then I won't have a job.
Tell me why.
She takes a breath. Salvi pays me two hundred dollars a month. It's in an envelope in my flat, every dollar of it. I've never spent any. I don't know what I was keeping it for. Evidence, maybe.
Somebody let themselves into the union back office at one in the morning and took Bask's notebook. A woman's heels.

She is quiet for a long time. Bask gave me a key on the 9th. He said: Etta, if anything happens to me, take the notebook to the city office. My name is on every page of it. I took it and I hid it. I went to the chapel afterwards and put the key in the poor box, and I have not slept since.
Did Bask come to see you?
On the 9th. He asked to see the Corvina manifest. I showed him. He read it and said: Etta, your name is on this. I said: I know.
Dov is a decent man. Decent men don't run harbours.
Miss Wren buys nothing from me. Inspectors don't need rope.
Salvi's crews buy the best rope, pay in cash, and never come back for the same length twice.
Mrs. Rask buys lamp oil every week for a lamp nobody needs. I don't charge her.
Garrow buys nothing. The lighthouse supplies him. He comes in to talk. He talks about 1941.
The doctor stitched my hand on the 12th and didn't ask how I'd cut it. I told her rope. She let me.
Ledoux buys rope by the hundred feet and never buys nets. Work that out for yourself.
I shut the shop at eight. The Dockside Café until ten. Then home. Nobody can confirm the last part.
You owed Bask two thousand dollars.
For a boat that sank in 1945 with everything I had on it. He lent me the money for it. On the 9th he demanded it back. I told him I couldn't pay. He said he knew that.
Forty feet of line and a sailmaker's needle, signed B.O. in your own sales book.
He closes his eyes. A man came in at closing time with his hood up. He put his hand over mine and said: sign it yourself. So I did. I sell rope. I didn't sew anything.
You know who it was.

I sell to every boat in this harbour. I know every hand that comes over my counter. He smelled of the ice house, and he had a boat, and I owe money to the man who owns that boat. That is all I am going to say, and I am ashamed of it.
Your rigging knife was redeemed at Lundy's on the 10th. You didn't redeem it.

I sold the ticket for two dollars on the 10th to eat. To a man off the trawlers, on the quay, in the dark. I didn't look at him. When you sell your own knife for two dollars you don't look at anybody.
Your hand is bandaged.
Rope. On the 12th, in the shop. He looks at it. I know what it looks like. I know what the doctor thought. It was rope.
Hollis will make a fine chairman. Reasonable. I like reasonable.
Miss Wren is a professional. I admire professionals.
Okafor is in debt. Men in debt are useful. That isn't a crime.
The widow blames everyone for a boat that sank before I ever came here.
Garrow is a public servant. I make contributions to public servants.
The doctor can't be bought. I've checked.
Ledoux fishes. What he catches is his business, and mine.
In my office, doing the accounts. The lamp was on until dawn. Anyone on the quay can tell you.
A strike on Thursday would finish you.
A strike would finish everybody. I'm nothing special. I have three ships and two of them only exist on paper. If the berths close, I'm a man with an office and nothing in it.
At midnight somebody with a key added a second set of initials to the Corvina manifest, with a broad-nibbed pen. Yours.

He looks at the pen on his desk for a long time. The lamp was on. I wasn't under it. I walked to the Customs House and made the crate look as if it had been approved twice, because Bask had copied the manifest and I wanted the paper to be perfect when he read it out. I didn't know he would never read anything out again.
You ordered two blocks of ice at three in the morning.
For the back room. For cargo. Cargo that spoils. He looks at the door. It wasn't Bask, if that's what you're asking. Bask was already in the water by then.
'Stop at the usual place.' That message went out from your office at four minutes past one.
The usual place is the ice house steps. Every boat that lands without Customs lands there. I sent it. It was about cargo. He does not say what the cargo was.
Dov Hollis carried my husband's coffin and then carried Bask's bags for eleven years.
The girl at Customs wouldn't look at me in 1941. She looks at me now. That's something.
Bernard brings me lamp oil and won't take money for it. It's the kind men who drown.
Salvi came to this harbour in 1942. One year after Ambrose. I've never trusted the timing.
Garrow was on Ambrose's boat. He came back. Ambrose didn't. Draw your own line between those two facts.
The doctor loved Bask. Everyone thinks I don't know. I've been a widow. I know what it looks like.
Ledoux was a boy on my husband's boat in 1941. He was sick over the side. He hasn't been sick since.
Here, at home. I don't go out after dark. Everyone on the point knows that.
Bask's name was written in chalk on the chapel plaque at half past four in the morning. Before his body was found.

She doesn't blink. I went out. Somebody came to my gate at a quarter past four and told me he was in the water. I put my coat on, walked to the chapel, and wrote his name under Ambrose's. I'm not sorry.
Who came to your gate?

A man in an oilskin with the hood up. He wouldn't come in. I didn't see his face. I saw his hands on my gatepost in the lamp. They were cut across the fingers, both of them, the way hands are cut when a man sews canvas without a palm.
Tell me about the letter in your drawer, from 1941.
Ambrose wrote it the morning he went out. It says: if I end up in the water, it wasn't the water. Ask Bask. So I asked Bask. For seven years I asked Bask.
Hollis came up to the lighthouse once to ask what I saw in 1941. I told him nothing. He believed me. That's Hollis.
Miss Wren keeps a log by day and I keep one by night. Neither of us reads the other's.
Okafor sold me a lamp glass in 1939 and has been apologising for the price ever since.
Salvi sends fifty dollars up to the lighthouse at Christmas. And at other times.
Tilda Rask has stared at this tower every night for seven years. I can feel it.
The doctor came up here in 1941 to sign a form. She looked at the water for a long time first.
Ledoux lands under the point with no lights. I write it down. Then I cross it out. Then I write it again in a book nobody knows about.
What did you see on the 11th?

The water. A trawler anchoring in the Narrows at ten past eleven with no lights. A rowing boat going from it to Pier Nine at a quarter past. The trawler going out at midnight and coming in at three. I wrote down what I'm paid to write down.
The entry about the rowing boat is crossed out. In your handwriting.

One man rowing to the pier. One man rowing back at ten to twelve. I crossed it out because fifty dollars came up the stairs the next morning in an envelope with no name on it. The money is on the shelf. I haven't touched it.
You keep a second log.
Under the floorboards. Everything since 1941. Every boat without lights. Every name I could put to one. Take it. I've carried it long enough.
Where do the boats without lights land?
The old salt stairs, cut into the point under my lamp. They are not on any map the police have. There is a man sleeping in them this winter. Big, fair, foreign. I have not written him down either.
You were on Ambrose Rask's boat.

I was. Ambrose went over the side. Bask was at the wheel. I was being sick in the bottom of the boat, next to a boy who was being sick harder. I didn't see who pushed him. I saw who didn't pull him back.
Dov Hollis has a bad heart and a good one. I treat the first.
Etta Wren came to me with a rash from worrying. I told her to spend the money. She didn't.
Bernard Okafor hasn't slept since 1945. I stitched his hand on the 12th. He said rope. I let him say it.
Salvi has never been ill a day in his life. Men like that are sick in other ways.
Tilda Rask should have been in my care years ago. Grief isn't an illness. It's a climate.
Garrow drinks. Not much. Just enough to cross things out.
Ledoux's hands shake in the mornings and not at sea. I know what that means.
At the Infirmary all night. Nurse Ives will confirm it. She'll also tell you I went out at half past five in the morning for an hour, when Kite telephoned. She's honest.
You wrote 'drowning' on the certificate. Then you wrote the truth over it.

I wrote drowning at twenty to six because that's what it looked like and because I couldn't look properly. I looked again at twenty past. The wound went upward. I wrote it down. That isn't a crime. It's the opposite of one.
Tell me about the hour you were out.
She looks at her hands. At the morgue, with him. I stood in the salt and looked at him for an hour. Then I washed my hands and did my job.
What was Bask to you?
A patient. Then more than a patient. Four years. Nobody in this harbour knew, which tells you how good the harbour is at knowing things.
He came to you at ten on the 11th.

He said somebody had offered to show him the hold of a boat, at Pier Nine, at half past eleven. Proof for Thursday. He wouldn't tell me who. He said: a man who was on the boat in '41, who wants to put it right. I told him not to go. He went.
He once asked you how a man is killed with a knife under the ribs.

Over dinner, months ago. Ledoux was there too. I told them: from below, upward, toward the heart. I thought Bask was asking so he could see it coming. He didn't see it coming. Somebody else at that table was listening better than he was.
Hollis never came down to the boats. Bask came every week. That's the difference between them.
The inspector signs. I sail. Neither of us looks in the hold.
Okafor sells me rope and looks at me as if I'm going to hang myself with it.
Salvi owns the boat. On paper the boat is mine. On paper I'm a fisherman.
The widow won't look at me. I was a boy on her husband's boat. I was seasick. That's all I did.
Garrow sees me land every time. He has never said a word. I sent fifty dollars up his stairs and it came back down.
The doctor is the only person in this harbour who ever asked me if I was all right. I said yes. It wasn't true.
At sea. Out at eleven, back at three. The harbourmaster has it in the log.
You went out empty and came back full.
Cargo. Off the Corvina, into the ice house. Salvi's cargo. I don't open it. I have a boat because I don't open it.
You anchored in the Narrows at ten past eleven, with no lights, and took the dinghy to Pier Nine.

He is quiet for a long time. I was to pick up a passenger for Salvi. A man who wanted to see the Corvina come alongside. I waited under the pier. He didn't come. I rowed back at ten to twelve and we went out. Pell will tell you the same. I was paid not to ask who the passenger was.
Your hands are cut across the fingers.
Line. Hauling in the dark. He puts them in his pockets. Every skipper in this harbour has hands like these. Ask Okafor about his.
'Stop at the usual place.'
The usual place is the ice house steps. Everyone who lands without lights lands there. We landed there at five past three and I unloaded until four.
You were a boy on Ambrose Rask's boat.
Fifteen. Sick over the side the whole way out. When I looked up he was in the water and Bask was at the wheel not turning it. I have never told anyone that. I am not sure why I am telling you.
A rigging knife in the drydock, bone handle, blade wiped clean.
This was in your window.

It was. Pledged by Okafor in March. Redeemed on the evening of the 10th by a man in an oilskin who had Okafor's ticket and paid cash that smelled of fish. Big hands, salt in the knuckles. I didn't see his face. He went down toward the trawler berths.
Your knife.

He looks at it a long time. Mine. I pawned it in March to eat. I sold the ticket on the 10th for two dollars to a man off the trawlers, in the dark, and I didn't look at him. Somebody paid my ticket, and then somebody used my knife.
A dented flask of rye, left on the bar at one.
Whose flask?
Dov Hollis's. He drinks from it when he thinks I cannot see. He was here from a quarter past midnight till one, and he was not drinking to celebrate.
Your flask. On Mags's bar at one.

I was at the Brine from a quarter past twelve. Before that the printers, before that the hall. I was drinking because I had paid a man four hundred dollars of union money to stand down and he had laughed at me. Mags saw me. Forty men saw me. Ask them.
A locket on the widow's desk, with a lock of hair inside.
Ambrose's?

His. Cut the morning he went out. I have had it seven years. I went out last night, Inspector. To the chapel. To write the name of the man who let my husband drown. A man came to my gate at a quarter past four and told me he was in the water. I wrote it. I did not put him there.
Whose hair?

Ambrose Rask's. She showed me once. She came to the chapel at half past four and chalked Bask's name and I let her. Whoever told her he was drowned told her before the tide did. Ask at the ice house who was walking toward the point at four.
A customs seal from bay four, broken in one twist.
Your seal. Your initials. Broken on the 11th.
She sits down. I initial. I do not open. Salvi pays me not to open and I have never spent a dollar of it. I was at the Customs House till eleven. Aldous saw me leave.
Who broke it?
Ledoux. At nine in the evening, on Salvi's word, before he sailed. One twist. He has done it before, on the Corvina crates, every month for six. He took a small case to the shipping office.
A brass button at Pier Nine, torn off with the thread still in it.
Whose coat?
A skipper's coat. We sell those buttons. We sold a set to Ledoux in January and he lost one in February. He came back for a match. We did not have one.
Yours.

He turns it over. Mine. I lost it on the ladder at Pier Nine, waiting for a passenger who never came. I slipped and went in to the waist and the button went with the ladder. That is all that happened on that ladder. He does not look up when he says it.
Bask's watch, salt in the works, stopped at twenty to midnight.
Eleven-forty. Does that fit?

It fits. The wound goes upward, so whoever did it was below him, on the ladder or in a boat. The pockets were sewn before he went in, so it took a quarter of an hour in a boat under the pier with a needle, in the dark. He looks at the watch. Whoever sewed those pockets has hands cut to ribbons this morning.
His watch stopped at eleven-forty.

She does not look at it. He came to me at ten. He said a man from the 1941 boat wanted to show him the Corvina's hold at Pier Nine at half past eleven. He asked me again how a man is killed with a knife under the ribs. I told him. I thought he was asking so he could avoid it.
Ashgrave Bay. The Ninth Bell.

Sister Constance Ayre rang the cathedral bell at midnight for twenty years. Last night it rang nine times instead of twelve, badly. At six in the morning the verger found her dead at the bottom of the tower stairs, hit from behind. The bell rope was cut. Whoever did it climbed down the outside of the tower. Her sister has been locked in Marrow House asylum for nine years. Nine strokes for nine years.
Inspector. Everyone. I came up the hill at a run. The verger at St. Ordell's found a nun dead at the bottom of the tower stairs an hour ago.
Sister Constance Ayre. Forty-four. She rang the cathedral bell at midnight every night for twenty years. Twelve strokes, never one more.

Last night the bell rang nine times, not twelve, and badly. Whoever rang it did not know how. By six this morning she was dead on the stairs with the back of her head broken and her keys still in her hand.

She did not fall. Somebody hit her from behind. The bell rope was cut on the ringing floor, and the person who did it did not come down the stairs. There are old iron rungs on the outside of the tower.
Her sister Beatrix has been a patient at Marrow House asylum for nine years, and the gate there was logged open at twenty to midnight. The Canon says the diocese would like discretion.
Note what the Canon wants, and then ignore it. You have two days. Start at the tower, and talk to the verger. He washed the stairs before we got there.
Sister Constance Ayre
Hill Division. The diocese has asked for discretion. Note it. Ignore it.
Marrow House asylum logged its gate open at eleven-forty and closed again at one.
The bell rope was cut clean. Whoever went up did not come down the stairs.

They ring twelve at midnight again, and the hill pretends that settles it. You stand in the wet grass under two hundred and eleven steps of cold stone and count to nine, once, for Constance Ayre. Then you go home.

The diocese gets its discretion. 'Accidental fall,' says the certificate, on stairs that turn the wrong way. The bell rings twelve. Somebody on this hill hears nine every night for the rest of their life. It is not you.

On the staff, or near enough. I see them across the quad every morning.

The gate is shut and I have a bell to ring in three hours.
Mr. Blake went out at half past eleven with two boys and came back at one. He signed nothing. He never does.
Dr. Quint sends a note down for the boys on clear nights. Friday was not clear. She sent the note anyway.
Who had a key that wasn't yours?
Harris, third form. He has the verger's tower key and the gate key both. He went out at eleven and came back at half past twelve without either.
Where is Harris now?

In the sanatorium at the back of the school, with a fever he has not got. It is a locked ward; nobody outside the school knows the door is there. He will not come out. He says a man took the key from him on the path by the reservoir and told him to forget it.
Did you know Sister Constance?
She rang for the school every morning at seven. Twelve strokes, then seven. Never one out. Friday morning nobody rang. That is how I knew before anyone told me.
They call me Mother Greer. Seventy-one years in this parish. I've buried two of the people on your list, and I'll bury a third.
I've known that one since they were small. Small people grow into big people. They don't turn into different ones.
I don't sleep. I heard the side door, and I saw somebody carry a bundle toward
I'm tired, child. Come back when it's light, and bring biscuits.
Sybil Crake was a nurse in this almshouse before she was a matron. She was kind then. Money is a hard thing to be kind through.
Peter Nane brings me tobacco and takes my advice, which is a fair trade. I told him to leave the Ayre girl alone. He did not.
Rosalind Fay's mother died in bed nine here. Rosalind drove the tram past the window every day for a year and never came in.
What did you hear?
Nine bells. Then the side door of this house. Then somebody on the path with a bundle, going down toward the water. Big steps. A man's.
What was in the bundle?
Something that clinked. Keys, or coins, or a rosary. He held it against his chest the way you hold something you should not have.

I taught her to ring. Sixty years ago I rang that bell myself. She came to me on Thursday and asked whether a person could be forgiven for something they signed. I said only if they unsigned it. She said she was going to try.
Marley. I sign the trams out and back in. The last car is at eleven. Tonight one went out at midnight and I didn't sign it.
They ride the last car. You learn a person by which seat they take.
A parcel came off the midnight tram and was left on the bench. Somebody carried it up to
The schedule is the schedule. I've said what I know.
Rosalind took car seven at a quarter to midnight with the lights off. I saw her hands on the brake from the office. She brought it back wet.
Mr. Blake rode down at one with two boys and a face like a funeral.
The Ayre woman got off car seven at the Close Green at ten past midnight. Alone. She had a bag. She did not have a ticket.
Car seven.
Out at a quarter to midnight, unsigned. Back at ten to one, wet. Rosalind Fay driving. One passenger up, from the Marrow House gate to the Close Green. None down.
A parcel came off the midnight car.
Left on the bench. A bag. Somebody carried it up the hill toward the cemetery at half past one. Not Rosalind. A man.
Did Sister Constance ride the tram?
Never. She walked. Two hundred and eleven steps up the tower and a mile down the hill and back every day for twenty years. She said the walk was the prayer.
Lister. I keep the boilers going so the orchids don't freeze. It's warmer in here than anywhere on the hill, so people come in.
They come in to get warm. You see a person clearly in this light.
Somebody burned something in my firebox tonight and didn't burn all of it. What was left went up the hill to
The boilers need me. The police don't.
Nane was here till two. He heard the bell and sat down on the coal and did not get up for an hour.
Dr. Quint sends down for orchids and I carry them up. Her dome smelled of chloral on Friday.
The Matron comes in to get warm on her way down from Marrow House. Friday she came in at one with river mud on her shoes.
What was burned in your firebox?
Paper. A ledger page, and a letter. Somebody came in at half past midnight, shoved them in and went. Not all of it burned. I pulled a corner out.
What was on it?
A number. Forty-four. And a signature in green ink. The Canon signs in green ink. Everybody on the hill knows that.
Wednesday. She stood in the warm for an hour and asked me whether the boilers could burn a ledger. I said they could burn anything. She said, good.
Grimm. I dig the graves. Tonight I found a hole I didn't dig, and I want to know who did.
They stand over the graves I dig. You see what a person is at a funeral.
Fresh earth was moved, and something was taken out, not put in. The cart tracks run to
I have a hole to fill and I've said too much already.
The verger tells Nane where to dig when I am drunk. I am drunk a good deal. I still know my own cemetery.
The Canon stood over plot forty-four on Tuesday evening with his hat off like there was somebody in it. There was not.
The hole you didn't dig.
Plot forty-four. Dug Tuesday by Nane, four feet, with a tin box in it. Dug up again Friday night by somebody in a hurry who left the box and took what was in it.
Cart tracks.
From the plot to the gate and down toward the water board. Somebody wheeled something heavy. Or somebody who could not walk straight.
Did Sister Constance come to the cemetery?
Every Sunday to her mother. Thursday she came and stood at plot forty-four for a long time and then she went to the Rectory. She walked like a woman going to a fight.
Ansell. My grandfather cast that bell. I've tuned it every Easter since I could hold a hammer. I know its voice. Last night somebody rang it who didn't.
They've been up the tower with me. You learn a person by how they climb.
A bolt from the bell clapper was taken from my bench last week. I found it this morning, dropped on the path toward
The furnace is lit. I'm not.
Cormac Ill has been up my tower a thousand times and cannot ring. He has no ear. Whoever rang nine had no ear either.
The Canon climbed the tower once, in 1928, and was sick at the top. He has not been up since.
You know the bell's voice.
Nine strokes, ragged. Rung by somebody who let go of the rope at the top of the pull. Not a ringer. Somebody who had watched ringing and never done it.
A clapper bolt was taken from your bench.
Last week. Found this morning on the path to the reservoir. Somebody wanted the bell silenced and then changed their mind and rang it anyway.
You knew Sister Constance.
Twenty years. The best ringer on the hill. She came to the foundry on Thursday and asked me how a rope is cut so it cannot be rung. I told her. I thought she was afraid of somebody.
Miss Pym. Four hundred years of parish records, and I've read all of them. Sister Constance came to me last week for the crypt account books. I gave them to her.
They read here. You can tell a person by which books they ask for.

The reading room closes at dusk, and it's long past dusk.
The Canon has not opened a parish register in ten years. He sent for the crypt ledger on Friday afternoon. I sent it. It came back with a page missing.
Mr. Blake reads the 1939 register. The year the Ayre girl was committed. He has read it three times.
Dr. Quint reads the weather records. Every clear night for a hundred years. She is looking for something in the sky. She has not found it.
A page was cut from the 1939 register.
The committal of Beatrix Ayre. Signed by the Canon, the Matron and Sister Constance. Cut out tonight by somebody with a razor and a key to this room.
Who has a key?
The Canon. The verger. And me. The razor was left on the desk. It was a barber's razor. Somebody who shaves with it, not a woman.
What did Sister Constance want from you?

The crypt ledger and the 1939 register. She read both here on Wednesday and made notes. She said, Dorcas, I signed my sister away for four hundred pounds and I did not even know it. She meant the Canon had taken the money. I think she meant more than that.
Oakes. I type the diocese's letters, including the one asking you to be discreet. I didn't agree with it.
They come before the Dean. You notice who is nervous in front of a bishop.

The Matron's quarterly report on the Ayre patient is the same every quarter, word for word. I have typed it thirty-six times.
Mr. Blake wrote to the Dean in March offering to resign. The Dean never answered. I never sent it.
A letter came for the Dean at one in the morning.
By hand. From the Rectory. The Dean burned it in the grate unread and told me to forget the hour. I have not forgotten it.
Where is the ash?
In the grate. I raked out one corner. It says: 'the ledger is in the crypt fund box and Constance has—'. That is where it burned.

Twice. Once about the schoolmaster, which she never sent. Once about the crypt fund and Marrow House, which she posted on Thursday. It has not arrived. Letters from the hill take a day. It should have arrived.

They come to this kitchen. You learn a person by how they look at the key board.

The younger Miss Ayre came to this kitchen on Wednesday and asked for the tower key. I said no. She looked at the key board a long time and then she looked at me.
The tower key.
Off its hook since Thursday. The verger lends it to a schoolboy. The boy did not bring it back. It came back this morning by itself, on the doorstep, with river mud on it.
River mud.
Reservoir mud. Black. It only comes from the wall walkway. Whoever put the key on my step had walked along the top of the dam in the dark.

Every night at half past eleven for the key, and every night at half past twelve to hang it back. Friday she came at half past eleven and it was not on the hook. She went up anyway. Somebody had already unlocked the door.

Dr. Quint buys chloral for herself. She says she cannot sleep. On Friday she bought twice the usual.

Nane. Lint and iodine. His hands were cut across the palms, both of them, like a man who had gripped a rope or a rung too hard. He paid with a wet coin.

Nothing, ever. Thursday she came in and asked to see the poisons book. She read the Matron's entries for nine years and said, that is a great deal of sleep for one woman.
Quaile. I do nights on the east ward. I know who's a real patient here and who's only wearing the gown.
They're on my ward, or they visit it. You learn a person by how they behave behind a locked door.

The Matron was in her office at midnight. I brought her tea. She was crying. I did not ask.
Beatrix Ayre is the sanest person in this building. I include the staff.
Mr. Blake came to the gate on Wednesday with a letter and a boy. The Matron would not take the letter. The boy gave it to me. I gave it to Beatrix.
The gate was open at eleven-forty.
I opened it. For Beatrix. With a bag. The Matron said let her go. She went down toward the tram.
Did she come back?
At dawn. Wet to the waist, no rosary, no bag. She got into her bed and she has not spoken since. Her hands are torn from rowing.
Did Sister Constance visit?

Thursday. First time in nine years. She sat with her sister for an hour. When she came out she went straight to the Matron's office and I heard the word 'papers' through the door nine times. I counted.
Hobb. Everything the hill is ashamed of comes through this door eventually. Last week it was a set of church keys.
They pawn things with me. I look at the hands that push them across the counter.

The church keys.
Pawned by the verger last week. Bought back at midnight on Friday by a different hand. Big hands. Cut across the palms. He paid with a coin from the reservoir, still wet.

Mr. Ill lends me the key. He thinks it is harmless. He is kind, and he is wrong.

The Canon is a good man with a bad ledger. I have kept his keys for twenty years. I have never kept his books.
The Matron comes to Mass and sits at the back. She looks at the Ayre pew the whole time.

I did. I found her at six and I could not leave her like that. I know what I did. I would do it again.

On the Close Green, under the tower. Looking up. The bell rang nine. I thought it was for me. I thought she was saying sorry.

She looks at her hands. I ran. Down to the reservoir. I took a boat. I lost my rosary and the oars and I rowed with my hands. I was on the far bank when the sun came up.

You sent your sister a letter.
Through Mr. Blake. It said: I know you signed it. I know why. Ring nine for me once and I will forgive you. She rang nine. Somebody rang nine.
The bell tower key, on the reservoir walkway, with river mud on it.

It is. It went missing on Thursday. The verger lends it to a boy from the Academy. He thinks I don't know. The boy meets a girl from Marrow House up there.
Your key. Found in the reservoir.
I lent it to a boy. Blake's boy, the tall one. He was to bring it back by eleven. He didn't. I was in my bed, Inspector. I found her at six and I washed the stairs because I could not look at them.
A rosary on the far bank, the beads wet, the cross bent.
Is this yours?
Mine. I dropped it in the boat. I rowed across because the tram driver would not take me back and I could not walk past the gate. I stood under the tower at midnight. I counted nine. Then I ran.

Inspector. All of you. It has happened again. A woman under a gas lamp on Gasworks Lane, found at ten to six this morning by a man on his way to the gasworks. I ran here from the lane.

Tell me about the three of them.

Ada Brill, thirty-six, seamstress, under Lamp 17 on Wick Street on the second of November. Nora Pask, twenty-three, dancer, under Lamp 29 at the canal bridge on the twentieth. Miriam Weiss, thirty-one, nurse, under Lamp 41 on Wednesday. Strangled, all three, with a cord. The lamp turned off first, every time, and the number in chalk on the pavement.
Is anything missing from your complaint book?
A page. From the week before Nora Pask died. Torn out clean. I found it on the twenty-first. Boyle was on the desk that week. I have not asked him yet. I was afraid of the answer.
What did the three women have in common?

Nothing I can find. Different ages, different work, different streets. Two of them lodged with Crowe. All three were treated at the Infirmary at one time. I keep coming back to 1946 and the fire, because all three were on Gasworks Lane that winter, but the fire was an accident and the inquiry said so.
