Peg Dwyer. I have the room next to Miriam's. Had. I heard her go out at six for her shift, same as always, and I did not hear her come back, because she did not.
This is a house of women. We notice the men who come to the door, because there are not supposed to be any.
Miriam kept a letter under her mattress that she would not show anybody. I think she took it with her on Wednesday. Try
Mrs. Crowe will hear us through the wall. She hears everything through the wall. Go.
Mrs. Crowe steams the post open. Everybody knows. Ada told her to her face in October and she did not even blush.
The constable walked Miriam home twice and stood at the gate like a dog. She sent him off kindly. He went.
Dr. Rowe came to see Ada's hand in '46 and never sent a bill. Ada said he was ashamed of something. She did not say what.
What happened on Wednesday?

Nothing happened here. That is the point. Mrs. Crowe went to bed at ten and snored. Nobody was ill. Nobody sent for anybody. If a note went to the Infirmary saying the landlady was ill, it was a lie, and somebody knew Miriam would believe it.
Does Mrs. Crowe read the post?

She steams it. Ada caught her at it in October and said so in front of all of us at breakfast. Mrs. Crowe said it was a precaution. Ada said: a precaution against what, Hattie, and Mrs. Crowe went red and said: against men who come to the door asking which room. Then she stopped talking.
A man came to the door asking which room.

In October. I was on the stairs. Tall, grey, a good coat gone shabby, very polite. He asked for Miss Brill's room and Mrs. Crowe told him for a shilling. He said thank you and he did not go up. He just went away. Three weeks later Ada was dead. Mrs. Crowe told the police nobody came. I did not say anything, because I am a coward and she is my landlady.
Tell me about Ada Brill.

She ran the sewing works with her sisters and she lodged here because the works has no rooms. She had a girl, Kitty. She lived on Gasworks Lane before the fire and she talked about it once, when she had been drinking. She said she had told the inspector twice about the smell of gas and she had said so at the inquiry, and she wished she had not, because it finished him. She said: he was not a bad man, Peg. He just did not listen.
Brother Amos. I ladle the soup and lock the door at nine and unlock it for anybody who knocks. Sister Agatha says that is the whole of religion. I am inclined to agree.
They all come to the door sooner or later. Hungry, drunk or ashamed. You learn a person from which.
Somebody came to the door at half past midnight on Wednesday and asked for a bandage for his hands, and would not come in. He went off toward
The soup is on. Come back when it is off.
Sister Agatha does things with the coal that the parish would not like. The parish does not feed forty a night. I keep my mouth shut.
The constable came in at one and was asleep by five past. Sister let him. I would have kicked him out. That is why she is the nun and I am the ladle.
Vane comes for soup at six and is drunk by nine. On Wednesday he did not come for soup. He was in the Gas Lamp by then.
Who came to the mission on Wednesday night?

Forty for soup. The constable at one, asleep by five past. And at half past midnight a knock: a man asking for a bandage for his hands. He would not come into the light. Tall. I gave him lint through the door and he said thank you very properly and went.
What was wrong with his hands?

Cord burns across the palms. I have seen them on dockers when a rope runs. He held them out into the lamplight and I saw them and then he took them back. He went off toward the gasworks, along the canal, not the lane.
Were you here for the fire in 1946?

I carried the Kane children out. Sister laid them out in the back room with Mrs. Penhale. The inspector sat by the stove all night and said nothing. Then the inquiry, and he was gone. Sister still prays for him. I still see his face by the stove.
Tom Gurney. This is the lamplighter's pub. Vane drinks here, and if you are asking whether he was here on Wednesday, the answer is yes, and the answer is also that he is not your man.
Forty regulars and I know what each one drinks and what he owes.
A man I did not know came in at nine on Wednesday, bought a bottle of the cheapest rum and asked me for a lamplighter's cord. I said I sell beer. He went toward
I have said it three times. It does not get truer.
Vane was on that stool from twenty to eleven until I put him out at half past twelve. He could not have turned off a tap, never mind a lamp.
Boyle comes in for a lemonade at ten and looks at Vane and does not write him up. Good boy. Bad constable.

Pask drinks here after the last tram. On Wednesday he came in at a quarter to one, white as milk, and said a lamp on the lane was out. Then he heard about the nurse and put his glass down and went home.
Was Vane here on Wednesday?

From twenty to eleven until I put him out at half past twelve. Drunk by eleven. His pole was not with him. The boy had it. The boy does his round for him most nights, and everybody in the ward knows it except the Gas Company.
Somebody asked you for a lamplighter's cord.

At nine on Wednesday. A tall man, grey, a good coat gone to the bad. He bought rum and asked where a man buys a lamplighter's cord. I said Ziegler's has one in the window with the pole. He said thank you and went. Very polite. I remember thinking: that is a man who used to be somebody.
Tell me about the boy.

Dickie. Fourteen. Vane pays him two shillings a night. He did Gasworks Lane at half past eleven on Wednesday with Vane's pole, and he swears every lamp was lit when he left it. Then he came here for his two shillings, and Vane had drunk them.
Nunn. I keep the poisons book and I keep it honestly, which is more than the last chemist did. Ask me what you like. I will tell you what I sold and to whom.
They all sign my book sooner or later. You learn a person from what they buy at night.
A man bought lint and iodine on Thursday morning at seven, before I had the shutters up. Cord burns on both hands. He paid and went toward
I have a queue. Come back at closing.
Dr. Rowe buys his chloral here rather than at the Infirmary, where they would count it.
Mrs. Crowe buys a sleeping draught every week and does not, I think, take it herself.
Sister Agatha buys iodine by the pint for the mission and argues about the price of every pint.
What did you sell on Wednesday?

Nothing that matters, on Wednesday. On Thursday at seven a man knocked before I had opened. Lint, iodine, a roll of bandage. Both hands cut across the palms in a line, the way a cord cuts when it is pulled hard. He did not wince. He paid in coins that had been in a drawer a long time.
Describe him.

Tall. Grey. A good coat, ten years old. He spoke like a man who used to give orders. I said: you should see the doctor. He said: I have seen the doctor, and he did not smile when he said it. He went toward the gasworks.
Do you sell blue chalk?
Tailor's chalk? No. The market sells it, and the sewing works buys it by the box. The police asked me the same thing in November. I told them the same.
May Aldridge. The nurses come in at seven when the shift ends. Miriam sat at that table every morning for four years. On Thursday the table was empty and I knew before anybody told me.
They come in tired and they come in honest. You learn a person at seven in the morning.
A boy came in at eleven on Wednesday with a penny and asked which way the Infirmary was. He had a folded note. He came from the direction of
The urn is boiling over. Come back.
Ned Boyle eats here for nothing because he has no money and no mother. He was sweet on Miriam. Everybody knew. She was kind about it.
Dr. Rowe takes his tea black and reads the death notices before the news.
Vane comes in at six in the morning, sober, and is the nicest man in the ward for one hour.
Did anything happen on Wednesday night?

A boy came in at eleven, out of breath, with a folded note and a penny. He asked which way the Infirmary was. I told him. I asked who the note was for. He said: the nurse, and a man gave me sixpence to run it. He was gone before I could ask which man.
One of the market boys. They run errands for anybody with sixpence. Rosa Benedetti at the chalk stall knows them all by name.
Tell me about Miriam Weiss.

Four years, every morning, tea and one slice, and a smile for anybody who needed one. She told me once she had nursed two children in the fire in '46 and had never got over it. She said: May, I told the inquiry what I saw, and it finished a man, and I still see his face. She did not say his name. I wish she had.

Miss Tench. I keep the ward archive. Every lamp has a card and every man who ever lit or inspected one has a card, and I can find any of them in under a minute. The Company would rather I could not find some of them.
They all come to this counter to complain about a lamp. You learn a person from how they complain.
Somebody has been reading the old inspection cards. There is dust on every drawer but one, and a boot print on the floor under it. The print went out toward
The Company is listening. Come back when it is not.
Vane has been docked three times for lamps out. All three complaints came from women who are now dead. I noticed that in November. The Company told me not to notice it.
Dr. Rowe gave evidence for the Company at the inquiry. His fee is in my ledger. Forty pounds. For saying a pipe looked sound.
The constable came in on Thursday and asked for the card on Lamp 41. He did not ask for the card on the man who used to inspect it.
Who turns a gas lamp off?

The lamplighter, with his pole, from the top. Or an inspector, at the base valve, with a key. The Company has had no inspector in this ward since December 1946. There were seven inspector's keys. Six came back. The seventh was never returned, and the card says it was lost in the fire.
The inspector who was dismissed in 1946. What was his name?

She takes a card out of the drawer without looking. Arthur Penhale. Inspector of lamps and mains, Wards district, 1926 to 1946. Dismissed after the Gasworks Lane fire. His wife died in it. His key was number seven. The card says he went to the country. She puts the card down. I do not think he went to the country. Somebody has been reading his old cards, and it was not the police.
Where would a dismissed inspector go, if he did not go to the country?

She looks at the window that faces the gasworks. The old retort house. Bricked up in 1944, at the back, behind the second gasholder. Every inspector had a key to it. It is not on the Company's map any more, because the Company does not like to remember it. If a man wanted to live where nobody would look, he would live there.
Big Jim Halloway. I found her. I walk down the lane to the six o'clock every morning, under the lamps, and on Thursday one of them was out and she was under it.
I see them on the lane at six in the morning. You learn a man from what he looks like before the day has started.
There is a stove burning somewhere at the back of the works that is not ours. I smell it on the night shift. It is over toward
The retorts want feeding. Come back at the change.
Vane's lamps are out half the time and he is drunk all the time. He is not a killer. He cannot climb his own ladder.
Boyle came running when I shouted. He was coming from the mission, not from the lane. He had bench marks on his face.
Pask's tram passed that lamp at ten to twelve. I know because I heard it from my bed. It did not stop.
Tell me what you found.

Lamp 41 out, and her under it, on her side, like she had lain down. A cord round her neck, the kind the lamplighters use to tie the ladder. The number 41 on the pavement in blue chalk, neat, like a man who has written numbers on pavements all his life. And a brass key by her hand. I did not touch it.
You smell a stove at the back of the works.

Coke smoke, at night, from behind the second holder, where the old retort house is. There is nothing there. It has been bricked up since the war. Somebody is burning coke in a place that does not exist, and the foreman says I imagine it.
Were you at the works for the fire in 1946?

I was on shift. The main on the lane went up like a match. The inspector, Penhale, came running from the office in his shirt and went into the building for his wife and they carried him out. Then they blamed him. Then he was gone. I liked him. He was the only Company man who ever came onto the floor.
Amos Wright. I keep the lock. The towpath runs from my door to the gasworks with no lamps on it at all, and on Wednesday night a man walked it twice.
The towpath is where the ward walks when it does not want to be seen. You learn a man from how he walks in the dark.
The man on the towpath dropped something at the bend at half past twelve. I heard it hit the stones. In the morning it was gone, but there were boot marks toward
A boat is coming through. Come back after.
The constable is supposed to walk the towpath at two. He has not walked it since November. On Wednesday he was in the mission.
Pask walked the towpath on the night his wife died, looking for her. He found the constable finding her. I heard him from here.
Vane fell in the canal in October. I pulled him out. He is not a man who walks a towpath in the dark on purpose.
Who walked the towpath on Wednesday?

A tall man, at a quarter to twelve, going toward the lane. No lantern. No pole. Walking like a man who knows the path. Then the same man at half past twelve, coming back toward the gasworks, faster, holding his hands out from his sides as if they hurt.
His hands.

Held out from his sides, the way you hold a burn. He stopped at the bend and put them in the canal. I heard the water. Then he went on, past the works, toward the back, where there is nothing but the old retort house.
Nora Pask died at the bridge.

Under Lamp 29. I heard nothing that night, which I have never forgiven myself for. The lamp was out. I noticed it at eleven and thought: Vane. Everybody thinks: Vane. That is the point of it, I think. Somebody wants us to think Vane.
Rosa Benedetti. I sell chalk, needles, thread and buttons, and I know every boy in the market by name because I pay them to fetch my tea.
They all come through the market. You learn a person from how they haggle.
The boy who ran the note on Wednesday was paid sixpence by a man standing by the pawnshop window, looking at a lamplighter's pole. He went toward
I have customers. Come back when the stall is quiet.
Klein's boy buys ink here. Klein's broadsheet is a penny and my chalk is a penny and one of us is honest.
Mrs. Crowe buys buttons and haggles over every one as if buttons were the last thing between her and the poorhouse.
Mr. Marsh buys sequins by the pound for his dancers and pays cash without looking at me.
Who bought blue chalk on Wednesday?

A tall man, at half past nine. Grey. A good coat gone shabby. He bought one stick of blue tailor's chalk and paid with a coin so old it was black. He had bought one in October and one in the middle of November too. Same man, same coin, same one stick. I remember because nobody buys one stick.
A boy ran a note to the Infirmary on Wednesday.

Little Sam. The man with the chalk gave him sixpence at eleven and a folded paper and said: the nurse at the Infirmary, and run. Sam ran. The man walked off toward Gasworks Lane, slow, like a man with all night.
Who else buys blue chalk?

The sewing works, by the box. Brill's. Ada Brill bought it herself every month until November. Her sisters buy it now. That is why the police looked at the sewing works first, and found three grieving women and nothing else.
Ziegler. Everything in this ward ends up in my window sooner or later. In October a lamplighter's pole and cord came in. In November the cord went out. I have been waiting for somebody to ask.
They all pledge something sooner or later. You learn a person from what they cannot bear to lose.
The man who bought the cords looked at a photograph in my window for a long time before he came in. A photograph of the fire. It came from
I have a customer. Come back.
Vane pledged his spare pole and cord in October for drink. He has not redeemed them. He does not need them; the boy uses his good one.
Marsh pawned a ring in November that was not his. It was Nora Pask's. He redeemed it the day after she died.
Klein pledged his second press in November to buy paper for the broadsheets. He redeemed it in a week. The broadsheets paid.
The lamplighter's cord.

Vane pledged a pole and three cords in October. On the thirtieth of October a man bought one cord off me for a shilling. On the nineteenth of November he bought another. On Wednesday at half past nine, the third. He did not buy the pole. He said he did not need the pole. Tall, grey, polite, hands like an old man's.
He looked at a photograph in your window.

A photograph of Gasworks Lane the morning after the fire in '46, that Klein printed and I framed because it sold. He stood in front of it for ten minutes. Then he came in and bought the cord and did not look at the photograph again. I took it out of the window the next day. I did not like how he looked at it.
Could Vane have taken his own cords back?
Vane could not find this shop by daylight. And I know a man's hands. The hands that bought the cords had never held a pole in their life. They had held a pen.
Ida Brace. I run the sheet. Every tram out and in, every driver, every minute. Walter Pask was on the last tram on Wednesday and the sheet says so, and so do I.
They all ride the tram. You learn a person from where they get off.
A tall man rode the last tram to the gasworks stop on Wednesday at half past eleven and did not ride back. He walked off toward
The eleven o'clock is late. Come back.
Walter was on the last tram from eleven until half past twelve. He came in white and said a lamp on the lane was out. He said it three times. Then he heard about the nurse.
Vane rides for nothing with his pole across his knees. On Wednesday the boy rode with the pole and Vane was nowhere.
Boyle rides to the mission at one every night and thinks I do not know where he gets off.
Who rode the last tram on Wednesday?

Pask driving, eleven to half past twelve. Six passengers. A tall grey man got on at the Alhambra at twenty past eleven and off at the gasworks stop at half past. He did not ride back. Walter said the lamp at 41 was out when he came past at ten to twelve. He said it three times.
The tall man.

A good coat, old. He sat at the back and looked at his hands. He got off at the gasworks and walked toward the lane, not the works. I thought: that is not a stoker. Stokers do not have coats like that, even old ones.
The night Nora Pask died.

Walter was on the last tram that night too. He got in at half past twelve and heard at one. He drove the next morning's first tram anyway. I should have stopped him. He drove it in a straight line and did not ring the bell once.
Sid Lark. Stage door. Nobody gets in or out of this hall at night without passing me, and I write them all down, because Mr. Marsh likes to know who his dancers leave with.
They come to the stage door for the girls. You learn a man from how long he waits.
A man stood across the road from this door on the nineteenth, the night before Nora died, and he was not Pask. He was watching Nora. He walked off after her toward
Curtain in ten minutes. Come back after.
Mr. Marsh was in his office from the curtain until one on Wednesday. I took him his tea at half past twelve. He was counting. He does not leave when he is counting.

Pask stood across the road every Saturday for a year. On the night Nora died he was there until a quarter past eleven and then he went to drive his tram, and she came out at half past, and I let her walk home alone because I always did.
Dr. Rowe comes to the second show on Fridays and sits at the back and signs the girls' certificates on Mondays.
Where was Marsh on Wednesday?

In his office from a quarter to twelve, when the curtain came down, until one. I took him tea at half past twelve. He was counting the take and swearing. He did not go out. I would know. The only door is mine.

She left at half past eleven, alone, toward the canal. Pask had gone at a quarter past to drive his tram. A tall man had been standing further up, by the pawnshop, since ten. Not Pask. When she went, he went. I wrote down: tall man, grey, followed N.P. I showed the constable. He did not write it in his book.
Nora went to the police about Marsh.

The week before. He hit her in the dressing room and she went to the station with the bruise. She came back and said the constable had written it down. Then Mr. Marsh went to the station too, and came back smiling. I do not know what happened. I can guess.
Cobbett. Night porter. I let people in and I let people out and on Wednesday I let Nurse Weiss out at twenty to twelve with a note in her hand, and I have not slept since.
They come through my door at night when they are frightened. You learn a person from how they ask for a doctor.
The boy who brought the note said the man who sent him was waiting under a lamp on Gasworks Lane. He pointed. He pointed toward
I have the door to mind. Go.
Dr. Rowe read the note over her shoulder and said: go on, Miriam, go. He did not read it. He never reads anything. He signs.
The constable walked her home twice and she told him to stop. He stopped. On Wednesday I wished he had not.
Mrs. Crowe has never been ill in her life. If the note said she was, whoever wrote it had never met her.
Tell me about the note.

A boy at twenty past eleven, out of breath, with a folded paper. For Nurse Weiss. It said: Your landlady has been taken ill. Come home at once. No name. She showed the doctor, he said go, she went. Out of the side gate at twenty to twelve, toward Gasworks Lane, because that is the short way to Wick Street. Under Lamp 41.
What did the boy say?

I asked him who sent it. He said: a tall man, sixpence, under the lamp on the lane. He pointed up the lane. Then he ran. I have thought since: the man was standing under the lamp where he was going to do it, sending for her.
Was Miriam here for the fire in 1946?

Her first year. She nursed the two Kane children for a night and a day and they died anyway. She gave evidence at the inquiry about the burns. She told me once she had said the burns were from gas, because they were, and that a man had lost everything because of it, and that she would say it again because it was true. She was like that.
Davy Rusk. I set the type. I set the nurse's name on Thursday morning at half past six while Mr. Klein stood over me, and I have set three dead women now and I would like to stop.
They come in to complain about what we printed. You learn a person from what they want taken out.
Mr. Klein keeps the original of the Lamplighter letter in the safe. There is no original. There is a draft, in his hand, and a proof. He burned the proof in the stove at
The press is running. I cannot hear you.
Mr. Klein wrote the letter. I set it. I know his hand and I set his hand. He has not said so and I have not said so and now I have.
Pask stood in front of the press and I hid under the bench. I am not proud of it.
The constable buys two sheets and tells the milkman everything. The milkman tells us. That is how we know about the chalk.
Where was Klein on Wednesday night?

Here, with me, until two, setting Thursday's sheet. Then at six the milkman said the nurse, and we set her name, and it was on the street by seven. He was here. He is always here. The press does not stop.
The Lamplighter letter.

He looks at the floor. Mr. Klein wrote it. On the third of November, at that desk. I set it from his draft. The Herald printed it as if it had come in the post. Nobody ever sent a letter. The killer does not write letters. He writes numbers, in chalk, and that is all he has ever written.
Klein printed a photograph of the fire.

In '46, for the Herald. We still have the block. The inspector is in it, at the edge, in his shirt, being held back. Mr. Klein cut him out of the print. He said it was not decent. I have the block with him in it. Nobody has asked.
Frye. All three came through here. I keep my own notes, because the doctor's certificates say what the Company would like and mine say what I saw.
They come here to look at the dead. You learn a person from what they look at first.
Ada Brill had a slip of paper in her shoe that the constable did not find and I did. A card from the Gas Company archive, with a lamp number on it. I gave it to the sergeant, who put it in a file at
I have three of them to look after. Go and find the fourth before I have to.

Dr. Rowe writes 'strangulation' and signs. He does not write what I write: that the cord was tied with a lamplighter's hitch, the knot they use on ladders, and that whoever tied it had tied a thousand.
The constable was sick in my sink twice. He looks at the faces. That is the wrong thing to look at. I told him: look at the hands.
Pask came to see his wife and stood for an hour and did not touch her. Then he hit the porter. I understood both.
Tell me what you saw on the three of them.

The same cord, three times: waxed lamplighter's cord, tied with the hitch they use for ladders. The same blue chalk on the fingers of the right hand, where he had held their hands to the pavement to write the number. And the same thing under their nails: not skin. Coke dust. Black, greasy, the kind from a stove that burns gasworks coke.
Coke dust.

Under the nails of all three. They clawed at his hands and his hands were black with it. A man who feeds a coke stove with his bare hands, every night. There is one stove in this ward that burns Company coke and is not the Company's. The coal merchant delivers to it.
Were the fire dead brought here in 1946?

The two Kane children and Mary Penhale. I washed all three. Her husband came at midnight and sat with her until they made him leave. He did not cry. He held her hand and looked at the wall. I have thought about his face more than I have thought about most living men's.
Miss Marlow. Every Herald since 1890 is on those shelves, and every one about the fire of 1946 has been read so often this winter that the pages are soft. Not by me.
They come here to read what the ward says about them. You learn a person from which page they turn to.
The Herald's report on the inquiry names three witnesses. The full transcript is not here. It is at
This is a reading room. Read.
Klein comes in to read what the Herald printed of his letter and goes out looking ill. Guilt reads slowly.
Dr. Rowe read the inquiry report in November and tore his name out of it. I have the page. It was the Company's paper, not mine.
Sister Agatha reads the deaths and prays over them at the table. She prayed over Mary Penhale's in '46 for an hour.
Who has been reading about the fire?

A tall grey man, every evening in October, at the corner table. The Herald for December 1946: the fire, the inquest, the inquiry. He read the same three pages every night for three weeks. Then he stopped coming. Ada Brill died the week he stopped.
What do the three pages say?

That the main on Gasworks Lane leaked, that the inspector had signed it safe, and that three witnesses gave evidence against him: a Miss A. Brill, who had reported the smell of gas to him twice; a Miss N. Halvey, later Mrs. Pask, who had seen him drunk on the lane; and a Nurse M. Weiss, who dressed the burns. The inspector was dismissed. His name is in the report. I will not say it in this room. It is in the transcript at the Coroner's Court.
Is there a photograph of the fire?
Klein's. The Herald ran it with the inspector cut out. The uncut print is in the Company's archive, and the man who was cut out of it is the only person who has ever asked me for it.

Miss Roper. I teach forty children and I taught the two Kane children who died in the fire, and I teach Kitty Brill now, whose mother died under a lamp. This ward does not let a teacher forget anything.
I know them by their children. You learn a person from what their child will not say.
Kitty Brill drew a picture in November of a tall man at her mother's door. She said he was the gas man. She drew him again this week, standing at
The bell has gone. Come back at four.
Sister Agatha keeps Kitty out of the orphanage by means I do not ask about. I would do the same.
Mrs. Crowe told me Kitty could not stay at the boarding house after her mother died. Women only, no children. She said it kindly. It was still cruel.
Klein's broadsheet is read aloud in my playground by children who cannot read. I have burned eleven of them.
What does Kitty Brill say?

That a tall gas man came to her mother's door in October and asked which room, and her mother said afterwards: that was Mr. Penhale, Kitty, from the lane, before the fire. He looked so old. That is what Kitty says her mother said. I told the constable in November. He wrote down 'gas man' and nothing else.
Tell me about the fire.

The Kane twins, seven. Top floor of the tenement. The gas came up through the floor in the night. Ada Brill lived below and got out with Kitty. Mrs. Penhale was visiting the Kanes and did not get out. The inspector had lived on the lane for twenty years and knew every family in it. After the inquiry he had no family and no lane. I saw him once more, at the cemetery, in '47, at night. Then never.
Blue chalk.

Tailor's chalk. The sewing works. I use white. The number on the pavement is written the way a Company man writes a lamp number on a post: the four with an open top. Nobody in my school writes a four like that. The Gas Company taught its men to.
Hobden. Coal and coke by the sack, delivered. I know every stove in the ward by what it burns, and there is one stove in this ward that should not exist and burns my best coke.
They all buy coal. You learn a person from whether they pay before the winter or after it.
The man who buys my coke for the place behind the works pays in old coins and carries the sack himself. He carries it along the towpath, toward
The cart is loaded. Come back tonight.
Sister Agatha sells me back the mission's coal at half price and buys coke with the money. I do not ask. I am not a priest.
Vane buys nothing. The Company heats his room and he drinks the difference.
The constable asked me in November whether I had sold rope. Rope. I sell coal.
The stove that should not exist.

Behind the gasworks, past the second holder, where the old retort house is bricked up. Since the spring of '47 a man has bought a sack of coke a week, cash, old coins, and carried it there himself on his shoulder. Tall. Grey. He does not give a name. I wrote him in the book as 'retort'.
Who is he?

I did not know for a year. Then one night I saw him in the lamplight and I knew. Penhale. The inspector. The one they blamed for the fire. He looked at me and I looked at him and neither of us said a word, and I have not said it since, because the man lost his wife and his name and I thought the least the ward owed him was to be left alone. I was wrong about that.
Black with coke, always. He feeds the stove bare-handed. On Thursday morning he came for his sack with both hands bandaged. He carried it anyway.
Bridget Kane. My boys died on the top floor of this building in December 1946. I still live on the second. People ask why. Where else would I live.
I have had every one of them at my door since the fire, with soup or a form. You learn a person from what they bring to a grieving house.
The night before Miriam Weiss died, somebody stood under Lamp 41 for an hour and looked up at my window. When the lamp went out he was gone. His boots went toward
I have said enough for one day. Come back tomorrow.
Dr. Rowe told the inquiry the pipes were sound. He came to my door a year later and could not look at me. I gave him tea. I do not know why.
Sister Agatha laid out my boys. I would give her my life. She does not want it.
Mrs. Crowe would not let me lodge with her after the fire. Widows with no children, she said, are bad luck. She said it to my face.
What did you see on Wednesday night?

Lamp 41 go out at a quarter to twelve. I was at the window. A tall man was standing under it with something in his hand, low down, at the base of the post, and then the lamp went out and he stepped back into the dark under the gasworks wall. I thought: Vane, and I went to bed. I went to bed.
Tell me about Arthur Penhale.

He lived on the ground floor for twenty years with Mary. He was the Company's inspector and he was ours too; he knew every pipe in this building. He told the Company the main was bad in the October. I know because Mary told me. The Company said spring. In December it burned. Mary was in my kitchen when it came up through the floor. Arthur went in for her. They blamed him. The three who spoke at the inquiry only said what they saw. It was the Company that killed my boys, and Arthur, and now it is Arthur killing the ones who spoke. I have known since the second one. God forgive me, I have known.
Where is he?

Where the Company cannot see him. Behind the works, in the old retort house, with a stove. He came to my door once, in '47, at night, and stood there, and I said: Arthur, go and live, and he said: I am trying to, Bridget, and he went. I did not know then what he was trying to do.
Sayer. I keep the coroner's files. The inquiry into the Gasworks Lane fire is in the basement, three boxes, and I can tell you now that nobody from the police has asked for it in two years.
They all give evidence here sooner or later. You learn a person from how they swear the oath.
The inspector kept a notebook of every lamp on his round, and it was entered as an exhibit at the inquiry. It was never returned. It went, with his key, to
The coroner is sitting. Come back after four.
Dr. Rowe swore the main was sound and took forty pounds from the Company that month. Both facts are in my files. Only one is in his.
The constable has given evidence at two inquests this winter and cried at both. The coroner was kind to him. I would not have been.
Mr. Marsh gave evidence at Nora Pask's inquest and lied about where he was. I know, because the doorman's book says otherwise and I have read it.
The inquiry into the fire of 1946.

Three boxes. Gas main, Gasworks Lane, leaked and ignited, the night of the fourth of December 1946. Two children and one woman dead. The Company's inspector, Arthur Penhale, found to have certified the main as sound. Dismissed. No prosecution. Three witnesses against him: Ada Brill, who had reported the smell twice; Nora Halvey, now Pask, who had seen him drunk; and Nurse Miriam Weiss, who dressed the burns and said they were from gas. He looks at you. Those are your three women, Inspector. I have been waiting two years for somebody to come down those stairs and ask me.
What became of Penhale?

Dismissed on the twentieth of December 1946. His wife buried on the twenty-second. He came to this office in January to ask for his notebook back and I could not give it to him, because it was an exhibit. He said: then keep it, and went. The Company says he went to the country. I have never believed it. A man who came back for his notebook is a man who stays.
Was the inquiry right?

No. He had reported the main twice, in writing. The Company's letters were not produced. Dr. Rowe said the pipes were sound. The three witnesses told the truth as they saw it and the Company arranged the truth around them. I took it all down in shorthand and I have never been asked for it until today.
Silas Bird. I dig the ward's graves and I know who visits which one and when. There is a grave here that is visited at night by a man who thinks nobody sees him. I see him.
They come to stand at graves. You learn a person from how long they stand.
The man who visits Mary Penhale's grave at night leaves the cemetery by the back gate, along the canal, toward
I have a grave to finish before dark. Go.
Sister Agatha buried the Kane children out of the mission's money and never told the parish. I dug for nothing.
Who visits at night?

Mary Penhale, died December 1946, row nine. Her husband comes every Sunday night after midnight and stands for an hour and puts a stone on the grave. He has put a hundred stones on it. He is tall and grey and he was not tall and grey in 1946. He thinks I do not see him. I have never once gone out to him. I am ashamed of that now.
Where does he go?

Out by the back gate and along the canal toward the gasworks. Not the lane. He does not use the lane, except when he does, and then somebody is dead under a lamp. He went that way on Wednesday at eleven. I have known since the second one what he is. I am telling you now.
A hundred stones.

One a week, since '47. Three of them are different: bigger, from the canal bed, put down in November and December. One after each woman. He is telling her. God help him, he thinks he is telling her something.
Vane lights lamps. He could not turn one off with a key if you showed him where the valve was.
Dr. Rowe gave evidence at the inquiry too. He said the pipes were sound. He was lying, and he is still alive, and he knows why.
The music hall man? I know nothing about him. I do not go to the music hall.
The nun took in the Brill child. That was a kindness. I have nothing against the child.
Pask married a woman who lied about me under oath. He should have asked her why.
The printer sells my name on every corner and has never once printed it right. They call me the Lamplighter. I put lamps out.
Mrs. Crowe let rooms to two of them. She let a room to my wife once, in 1938. She does not remember.
The constable sleeps in the mission. I have walked past him three times.
Where were you on Wednesday night?
He looks at the stove for a long time. Here. Where else would I be. I have been here two years. Nobody came to ask until you.

The main on Gasworks Lane was old. I said so, in writing, twice. The Company said it would hold until the spring. It did not hold. Two children and my wife. At the inquiry the Company said I had signed it safe, and three people stood up and said they had seen me drunk, or smelled gas and told me, or dressed the burns. All of it true and none of it the point.
Ada Brill, Nora Pask, Miriam Weiss. The three witnesses.

He nods, slowly. You found the file. Good. Somebody should have read it two years ago. He does not say anything else for a long time, and then: they said what they saw. I know that. I have always known that.
This is an inspector's key. P-7. Yours.
Mine. Twenty years in my pocket. He turns it over. I dropped it on Wednesday. I have never dropped it before. My hands are not what they were.
Why the lamps?

Because the Company put me in the dark and said it was my fault. Because the lamps were mine. Because a lamp turned off is a thing I know how to do, and there is very little else left that I know how to do.
The doctor signed my hand off in '46 when I burned it on the lane. He is all right.
Marsh lets me in the back of the Alhambra for nothing. I keep his lamps lit.
Sister Agatha gives me soup and a sermon. I take the soup.
Pask drives the last tram and I light the lamps in front of it. We have never spoken.
Klein printed my name on a broadsheet and sold it for a penny. I would like to sell him something for a penny.
Mrs. Crowe complained about the lamp outside her house every week for ten years. It was never that lamp.
Boyle is a good lad and a bad constable. He sleeps in the mission. Everybody knows.
The Gas Lamp. From twenty to eleven. Tom Gurney will tell you. I had done the round. Most of the round.
Most of the round.

He looks at his boots. The boy finished it. Dickie. He is fourteen and he does it better than me. He had my pole. He did Gasworks Lane at half past eleven, and every lamp on it was lit when he left it, he says. Then somebody put one out.
How do you turn a gas lamp off?
With the pole, from the top. You hook the chain. Or at the bottom, with the valve key, if you are an inspector and have one. Nobody has had one since Penhale, and he is gone.
Did you know the three women?

Brill complained about Lamp 17 for a year. Pask danced at the Alhambra and never looked at me. The nurse said good evening every night on Gasworks Lane and I said it back. That is all three of them. That is the whole of it.
Vane is a drunk with a burned hand. Not a murderer. Murderers are organised.
Marsh sends his dancers to me with bruises and pays cash. I write 'fall'.
The nun brings me the ward's dying and argues about the bills.
Pask came in on the twenty-first to see his wife's body and hit the porter. Grief.
Klein prints the death notices. He prints them before I have signed them.
Mrs. Crowe sent me a lodger with a rash every month for nine years. Never the same lodger.
Boyle brought me two of the three bodies. He was sick both times.
At the Infirmary until ten to midnight. Then I drove home. Cobbett at the door will tell you when I left. The garage will tell you when the car came in.
A note came for Nurse Weiss at twenty past eleven. You let her go.
A boy brought it. It said her landlady was ill. I told her to go. I did not read it. I should have read it. He looks at his hands. I have signed a great many things without reading them.
You told the 1946 inquiry the main was sound.

The Company asked me to. They paid the Infirmary's coal bill that winter. I looked at a pipe I did not understand and said it looked sound to me. A man lost his wife and his name because of it. I have not forgotten his name. Nobody else in this ward remembers it.
You treated all three of them.

Brill for a burned hand in '46. Pask for a broken toe last spring and other things I wrote down as falls. Weiss worked for me for four years. She was the best nurse I had. I sent her out into the dark with a note I had not read.
Vane lights my lamps outside for a free seat. He is harmless when he is sober, which is rarely.
Rowe writes what I ask him to write and charges me for it.
The nun stands outside my hall on Saturdays and prays at the queue.
Pask is a small man with a big grievance. He was right about the grievance.
Klein prints my bills. He also prints the broadsheets that empty my hall.
Mrs. Crowe would not let Nora lodge with her. Said dancers were trouble. She was right about that too.
Boyle owes me a favour. I do not intend to collect it from a policeman in front of a detective.
In the hall until the curtain at a quarter to twelve, then in my office with the take until one. Lark saw me. The take balanced, which it never does.
Tell me about Nora Pask.

She danced in the second show and she was the only reason anybody came to it. She was leaving me for the Empire in the city. I was angry. I am still angry. She is dead and I am still angry with her, which tells you what kind of man I am.
She went to the police about you the week before she died.

He puts the cane down. Yes. I hit her. Once. She went to the station and the constable wrote it down and I gave him five pounds to lose the page. That is what I did. I did not kill her. I would have had to leave my office to do that.
Did you know the three women knew each other?
Did they? Nora never said. She talked about the fire once. She said she had said something at an inquiry she wished she had not. She would not say what.
Cyrus Vane eats my soup and would not hurt a fly. He has hurt himself for thirty years.
Dr. Rowe sends me the ward's dying to save the Infirmary a bed. I take them.
Mr. Marsh runs a house of sin and gives me ten pounds at Christmas. I take that too.
Walter Pask came to me the night his wife died and could not stop shaking. I sat with him until dawn.
Klein prints my appeals for free and his broadsheets for a penny. God will sort it out.
Hattie Crowe lets rooms to women and reads their letters. I have told her it is a sin. She says it is a precaution.
Ned Boyle sleeps on my bench when he should be on the lane. On Wednesday I let him. I will answer for that.
Here. Forty for soup at six, beds at nine, prayers at midnight. The constable came in at one and fell asleep on the bench. I let him sleep. Somebody on Gasworks Lane could have used him.
You took in Ada Brill's daughter.
Kitty. Eight. Her mother died under a lamp in November and the parish wanted her for the orphanage. I said no. I have been saying no to the parish for thirty years.
The mission's coal goes to Hobden's yard. For money.

She does not look away. Yes. Six sacks a week, sold back to the man who gave them. The money keeps Kitty out of the orphanage. Ada found out in October. She sat where you are sitting and she said: Sister, God will understand, and so do I. Nobody else knows she said that.

I laid out the two Kane children and Mary Penhale in this room. Her husband sat where you are sitting and did not speak. Then the inquiry happened, and then he was gone. I have prayed for him every night since. I do not think it has reached him.
Vane lights the lamps in front of my tram. On Wednesday one of them on Gasworks Lane was out when I came past at ten to twelve. I noticed. I did not stop.
Rowe signed my wife's certificate in five minutes and charged me for the form.
Marsh. He is quiet for a long time. I have thought about killing Marsh every day for three weeks. I have not done it. I will not do it. That is the only thing I know for certain about myself now.
Sister Agatha sat with me the night Nora died. She did not say anything. It was the only thing anybody has done that helped.
Klein printed Nora's name in his broadsheet with a drawing of a lamp. I went to his shop. His boy hid.
Mrs. Crowe would not let Nora lodge there when we were courting. Dancers. She was not wrong about Nora and she was not kind either.
Boyle found Nora. He was sick on his boots. He is a boy in a uniform.
Driving. Eleven to half past twelve, the last tram, Wick Street to the gasworks and back twice. Mrs. Brace has it on the sheet. I passed Lamp 41 at ten to twelve and it was out.
The lamp was out at ten to twelve.

Out. Dark. I have driven past that lamp two hundred nights and it has never been out. I thought: Vane is drunk again. I did not think anything else. If I had stopped she would have been alive. I know that. You do not need to say it.
Tell me about the night your wife died.

I stood across the road from the Alhambra until a quarter past eleven, like a fool, watching the stage door. Then I drove the tram. She came out at half past, after I had gone, and walked home along the canal, and somebody was waiting at the bridge. I have never told anybody I was there. Now I have.
Nora gave evidence at the inquiry into the fire.

In '46, before we married. She said she had seen the inspector drunk on the lane. She told me later she was not sure it was him. She said it because the Company's lawyer asked her to and she was nineteen. She never forgave herself. I did not know it mattered to anyone else.
Vane came to my shop with a bottle and told me to stop printing his name. I stopped. I print 'the lamplighter' with a small L now.
Rowe sends me the death notices to set before the ink is dry on the certificate.
Marsh buys a hundred bills a week and complains about the price of every one.
Sister Agatha's appeals I print for nothing. She has never once thanked me. That is how I know she is a real nun.
Pask came in and stood in front of my press and did not say anything. My boy hid under the bench. I do not blame either of them.
Mrs. Crowe buys the broadsheet every morning and reads it to her lodgers at breakfast. Two of her lodgers are in it.
Boyle buys two. One to read, one to show the sergeant he has read it.
At the press with my son until two, setting Thursday's sheet. Davy will tell you. We had the nurse's name by half past six. The constable told the milkman and the milkman told my boy.
The letter to the Herald, signed 'The Lamplighter'. The fourth of November.

He sits down. I wrote it. On this press. There was no letter from anybody. I needed a name for the sheet and the Herald printed it and the whole ward said it back to me. I have sold thirty thousand sheets on a lie and I have not slept since the second one.
The chalk numbers. Did you print those?

No. Nobody outside the police knew about the chalk until the second one, and I only knew because Boyle told the milkman. Blue tailor's chalk. The sewing works uses it. The market sells it. It is the only true thing in my whole sheet.
Vane's lamp outside my door has been out more nights than it has been lit. I have written to the Company forty times.
Dr. Rowe comes when I send for him and charges the lodger, not me. A fair arrangement.
Marsh sent that dancer to my door for a room. I said no. I do not take theatricals.
Sister Agatha calls my reading of the post a sin. Sister Agatha has never had a lodger run off owing six weeks.
Pask I have met once, at my door, courting the dancer. I did not let him past it.
Klein's broadsheet is a penny and I buy it every day. I read it to the girls at breakfast so they know to be careful. Two of them were not careful enough.
Boyle walked Miriam home from the Infirmary twice in November. He was sweet on her. He did not walk her home on Wednesday.
In bed at ten. I was not ill. Nobody sent for a nurse. If a note said I was ill, somebody wrote it who knew where she lodged and knew she would come.
You read your lodgers' post.

I steam it and I read it and I seal it again. A precaution. I have had girls run off owing six weeks, and I have had girls with men writing to them who should not. Ada knew. Miriam knew. Neither of them left, which tells you it is not as bad as the nun says.
A man came to your door in October asking for Ada Brill.

She is quiet for a long time. I told the police nobody came. A man came. Tall. Grey. Polite. He asked which room was Miss Brill's and offered a shilling for the answer and I took it, because I thought he was a debt collector, and because it was a shilling. Three weeks later she was dead under Lamp 17. I have not slept in a bed since. I sleep in the chair by the door.

Ada and Miriam knew each other from the fire, in '46. Ada lived downstairs from it and Miriam nursed the children. They did not talk about it. Once, in the kitchen, Ada said: we should not have said it, Miri. Miriam said: we said what we saw. I did not ask what. I should have.
Vane is drunk by eleven every night. I have never once written him up. He lights the lamps in front of me and I let him.
Dr. Rowe told me to stop being sick at bodies or find another job. He was not unkind about it.
Marsh. He looks away. I took a complaint about him from Nora Pask. It is not in the book. I will tell you why if you make me.
Sister Agatha lets me sleep. She should not. I should not. On Wednesday she should have kicked me into the street.
Pask hit the porter at the Infirmary when he saw Nora. I did not book him. Some things you do not book.
I buy Klein's sheet. I told the milkman about the chalk and now it is in the sheet and the sergeant thinks I am a fool. The sergeant is right.
Mrs. Crowe told me to stop walking Miriam home. So did Miriam. I stopped.

On the beat. He stops. No. Gasworks Lane until midnight, then the mission. I sat down on the bench at one and I woke up at five. She was under my lamp the whole time. My lamp. I am supposed to say I was on the beat and I cannot.
Nora Pask made a complaint against Marsh and it is not in the book.

He goes white. Marsh gave me five pounds. I tore the page out. A week later she was dead under the bridge and I was the one who found her. I have the five pounds in my locker. I have not spent it. I do not know what to do with it.
You walked Miriam Weiss home.

Twice. In November. She was kind about it. She said: Ned, I am not afraid of the dark and I do not need a policeman, and she was right, and on Wednesday I was asleep on a bench. That is the whole of it.
You were on Gasworks Lane until midnight. What did you see?

Lamp 41 was out when I came past at a quarter to twelve. I thought: Vane. I did not stop. There was a man on the towpath below the lane, walking toward the gasworks with no lantern. Tall. I thought: stoker. I did not stop for him either.
A brass valve key by her hand, the kind that turns a gas lamp off at the base, stamped P-7.
Do you know this?

He turns it over. Inspector's key. For the valve at the bottom of the post. I have never had one. We had a man with one, before the fire. Penhale. P for Penhale, I suppose. Seven. He had the seventh. He is gone.
Whose key is this?

She does not need to look at the card. Number seven. Arthur Penhale, inspector, 1926 to 1946. Lost in the fire, the card says. It was not lost in the fire. It was in his pocket on Wednesday night, and now it is in yours. If you want him, he is where the Company does not look: the old retort house behind the second gasholder.
A stick of blue tailor's chalk from the market, worn to a wedge.
The numbers on the pavement.

Tailor's chalk, held like a pencil, and the four with an open top. That is a Gas Company four. They taught their men to write it that way on the posts so it could not be mistaken for a nine. Whoever writes these numbers was taught by the Company.
Your broadsheet says the chalk is a message.

I made that up. It is not a message. It is a lamp number, written the way a man writes lamp numbers. I have looked at the photograph of the 41 for an hour. It is neat. It is a working man's hand. It is not mine and it is not Vane's, and I have sold thirty thousand sheets saying it is.
A length of waxed lamplighter's cord from under the canal bridge, cut clean.
The same cord?

The same. Waxed, the Company's issue, cut from a longer piece with a knife and tied with the ladder hitch. Three women, three lengths, one hand tying them. A hand that has tied that hitch a thousand times, on a ladder, in the dark, at the top of a post.
One of yours?

One of Vane's. Cut from the coil he pledged. The second one I sold, on the nineteenth of November, to the tall man. I remember the cut end; I cut it myself. He asked me to. He said: about four feet. I did not think about why a man wants four feet of cord.
The note that brought Miriam Weiss out of the Infirmary: her landlady taken ill, come home at once.
Were you ill on Wednesday?

I have never been ill a day in my life and everybody in this ward knows it. Whoever wrote this did not know me. He knew her. He knew she would come running for an old woman she did not even like. That is a man who had watched her.
Do you know this hand?

Capitals, pencil, and look at the seven in "at once" — no, the four. There is no four. But the E: three bars, the middle one short. That is how the Company taught its men to letter a post. I have seen it on every lamp on Gasworks Lane for twenty years.
Nora Pask's wedding ring, pledged by another man and bought back the day after she died.
This is Nora's.

He closes his hand on it and does not open it again. She gave it to him. To Marsh. In November. She said she had lost it. I knew she had not. I have been driving a tram for three weeks with my hands shaking on the brake. Thank you for this. I mean it. Thank you.
You pawned her ring.

She gave it to me to prove she was leaving him. I pawned it because I was angry. I bought it back when she was dead because I was ashamed. Then I pawned it again because I could not look at it. That is the whole of me, in one ring, and none of it is murder.
The uncut photograph of the fire: the inspector at the edge, in his shirt, held back from the building.
Do you know this man?

She touches the edge of the print. Arthur. Going in for Mary. They held him. He did not fight them. He just looked at my window. He has looked like that ever since. That is the face that came to my door in '47. It is the face that stood under Lamp 41 on Wednesday, and I went to bed.
This man visits a grave here.

That is him. Younger. He was not grey then. He was grey by the spring. Row nine, Mary Penhale, every Sunday after midnight. He was there on Wednesday at eleven, and he left by the canal, toward the works, and I did not go out to him. Go out to him. Somebody should.
